docs.title: 🍅 tomato - behavioral testing toolkit
docs.text:
▶ Watch the one-minute introduction

Tomato is a language-agnostic behavioral testing framework that manages your test infrastructure automatically.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Built-in Container Orchestration - Automatically manage test containers with Testcontainers
  • Clean State Testing - Every resource is reset before every scenario for reliable, isolated tests
  • BDD/Gherkin Support - Write tests in plain English using Cucumber syntax
  • Multiple Resource Types - HTTP client (with Server-Sent Events) and server, gRPC client and server, PostgreSQL, ScyllaDB/Cassandra, Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ, S3, WebSocket client and server, Shell, a browser that uses the web UI in a real Chromium, and PDF documents the application generates
  • Presets - preset: kafka instead of a page of listener config, with MSK-style AWS_MSK_IAM authentication on the stock apache/kafka image
  • AWS identity - an aws resource gives the app IRSA against an STS tomato serves
  • Avro + Schema Registry - Publish and assert Kafka Avro messages as plain JSON
  • Web UI - tomato ui browses the suite, draws each scenario's flow and the topology of what it touches, and runs scenarios from the browser
  • CI Reports - JUnit XML and Cucumber JSON alongside console output
  • Step Coverage - tomato coverage reports which resource steps your features use, with --min to gate CI
  • Auto-generated Documentation - Keep step docs in sync with code
  • Application Runner - Start your app connected to test containers

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
tomato runs your application the way production does and talks to it over the network. A suite is tomato.yml plus .feature files — no glue code. Every scenario starts from the same state, because tomato resets every resource before each one and gives you no way to turn that off.

The part people miss: assert the effects. A 201 says your handler did not crash. Whether the row landed, the event published and the receipt was written is what the rest of your system depends on, and Writing a Suite is about asserting those.

docs.title: Stability and versioning
docs.text: tomato v2 is the current major version; the v1 branch no longer receives updates. This page defines what "stable" means for v2, so that promise can be kept, and so contributors know which changes need extra care.

docs.title: The stable surface
docs.text:
These are the parts of tomato that test suites depend on. Within v2 they change only in backwards-compatible ways, following the versioning and deprecation rules below.

Surface What is covered tomato.yml schema Every field documented in the Configuration Reference under version: 2, its meaning and its default Step vocabulary Every step listed by tomato steps (and on the resource pages): its wording, its arguments and what it asserts Resource types The type: names accepted by tomato validate, including aliases (postgresql, http-client, minio, …) CLI Commands init, run, validate, steps, coverage, version, update, their flags, and exit codes (0 pass, non-zero fail) Report formats The console formats and the junit and cucumber file outputs described under Reports GitHub Action Inputs of tomatool/tomato@v2: version, config, features, tags, scenario, verbose, quiet, skip-validate, comment Template variables {{.container.host}}, {{.container.port.N}} and {{.resource.url}} in app.env; {{.resource.address}}, {{.resource.host}} and {{.resource.port}} for a grpc-server

docs.title: Not covered
docs.text:
These can change in any release:

  • Go packages. Everything under internal/ and the command package. tomato is a binary, not a library; don't import it.
  • The tomato event format (--format tomato, TOMATO_EVENT: lines). It exists for the GitHub Action and the web UI. It becomes stable only when it is documented as a format for users.
  • The web UI (tomato ui) and hidden commands such as tomato docs.
  • Console output text: wording, colours and layout of pretty output and error messages. Parse the junit or cucumber outputs instead.
  • Default container images in tomato init templates.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
tomato follows Semantic Versioning for the stable surface:

  • Patch (2.1.x): bug fixes only. A fix may make a step stricter when it was wrongly passing; that is called out in the changelog.
  • Minor (2.x.0): new resources, steps, options and flags. Existing suites keep working. Deprecations are announced in minor releases.
  • Major (3.0.0): removals and incompatible changes. A new major also gets a new version: number in tomato.yml, so an old binary never misreads a new config: tomato rejects any version it doesn't support, with a link to this page.

A breaking change that still lands in a minor release is marked Breaking under Changed or Removed in the changelog.

docs.title: Deprecation policy
docs.text:
When part of the stable surface has to go:

  1. It is marked deprecated in a minor release, with its replacement named in the changelog and in the docs.
  2. It keeps working for at least one further minor release. Deprecated steps log a warning the first time they run in a suite (deprecated step: use … instead), and the generated step docs label them Deprecated.
  3. It is removed no earlier than the next minor release after that, or in the next major release.

Contributors: mark a step deprecated by setting Deprecated: "use … instead" on its StepDef. The step keeps its handler; tomato wraps it to emit the warning.

docs.title: The "at your own risk" warning
docs.text: Until October 2026 the README opened with a warning that v2 was under active development and should be used at your own risk. It was removed on 13 October 2026: v2 is the version tomato ships and the v1 branch is kept only for reference, so the stable surface above is now held to the versioning and deprecation rules on this page.

docs.title: Migrating from v1
docs.text:
tomato v1 (the v1 branch) no longer receives updates. v2 is a rewrite, not an upgrade in place:

v1 v2 No version field version: 2 at the top of tomato.yml resources: is a list of {name, type, options} resources: is a map keyed by name: app-client: {type: http, …} Types such as httpclient, http/client, queue + driver: rabbitmq, mysql, nsq, wiremock Types such as http, http-server, rabbitmq, postgres; MySQL, NSQ and Wiremock have no v2 equivalent yet (see tomato validate for the list) Connection strings (datasource) supplied by you, services started by you (e.g. docker-compose) containers: started by tomato; resources point at them with container: v1 step wording v2 step wording: run tomato steps

tomato recognises a v1 file (no version and a list under resources) and stops with a pointer to this section instead of a YAML decoding error.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text: Complete reference for tomato.yml configuration options.

docs.title: File structure
docs.text:
version: 2              # Required: config version

settings:               # Test execution settings
  timeout: 5m
  fail_fast: false
  output: pretty
  containers:
    reuse: false        # keep containers between runs instead of starting fresh

app:                    # Application under test (optional)
  command: ./my-app
  port: 8080
  ready:
    type: http
    path: /health
  wait: 5s
  env:
    KEY: value

containers:             # Container definitions
  name:
    image: image:tag
    command: []         # Optional startup command (list or string)
    env: {}
    ports: []
    volumes: []
    depends_on: []
    wait_for: {}

resources:              # Resource/handler definitions
  name:
    type: http|http-server|grpc|grpc-server|postgres|scylladb|cassandra|redis|kafka|rabbitmq|s3|websocket|websocket-server|shell|aws|lifecycle|browser|pdf|network
    # aliases: postgresql, http-client, grpc-client, websocket-client, minio
    container: container_name
    options: {}

hooks:                  # Lifecycle hooks
  before_all: []
  after_all: []
  before_scenario: []
  after_scenario: []

features:               # Feature file settings
  paths:
    - ./features
  tags: ""

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Field Type Default Description timeout duration 5m Global test timeout fail_fast bool false Stop on first failure output string pretty Output formats, comma-separated; see Reports

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
output takes one or more comma-separated formats. A format without a path prints to the console; format:path writes that format to a file. Use this to feed CI test reports and test-management tools.

settings:
  output: "pretty,junit:reports/tomato.xml,cucumber:reports/cucumber.json"
Format Writes pretty Human-readable console output (default) progress One character per step junit JUnit XML, one testsuite per feature and one testcase per scenario cucumber Cucumber JSON, the input most Cucumber report tools import tomato Structured events used by the GitHub Action's PR comment

Tomato creates the report directories if they don't exist. When --format is passed on the command line (the GitHub Action passes --format tomato for PR comments), it replaces the console format but file outputs from output are still written.

docs.title: The tomato event format
docs.text:
tomato writes one TOMATO_EVENT: line per event, followed by a JSON object with a type: feature_start, scenario_start, step_start, step_end, scenario_end, feature_end and summary. A step_end has the step's status, stepIndex, durationMs and, when it failed, its error text.

When a step failed because a value it compared did not match (stdout is:, response body is:, response json contains:, a Kafka, RabbitMQ or WebSocket message), its step_end also has a mismatch object with both sides, which tomato ui draws as a diff:

{"type": "step_end", "status": "failed", "error": "at status: expected created, got pending",
 "mismatch": {"what": "response JSON", "mode": "subset",
              "expected": "{\"status\": \"created\"}",
              "actual": "{\"id\": 1, \"status\": \"pending\"}"}}
Field Meaning what What was compared, such as stdout, body, message or response JSON expected The expected value as text, after variables are replaced actual The actual value as text mode text: compared as text. json: compared as JSON, every key on both sides. subset: compared as JSON, keys only actual has are allowed

error is the same text with or without mismatch. The field is left out when expected and actual together are over 256 KB. The event format is not part of the stable surface.

In the tomato format, a step_end event carries screenshots when the step left images behind, as a list of {"resource": "alice-browser", "path": "…/after-apply.png"}: the browser resource's saves screenshot, and the page when a step failed. tomato ui reads it to put the picture on the step.

docs.title: App configuration
docs.text:
Configure your application under test to run with test containers.

app:
  # Option 1: Run a command
  command: go run ./cmd/server
  workdir: ./

  # Option 2: Build from Dockerfile
  build:
    dockerfile: Dockerfile
    context: .

  # Connection settings
  port: 8080
  ready:
    type: http          # http, tcp, or exec
    path: /health       # For HTTP checks
    status: 200         # Expected status (default: 200)
    timeout: 30s        # Ready check timeout

  # Wait after ready check passes
  wait: 5s

  # Environment variables (supports container templates)
  env:
    DATABASE_URL: "postgres://test:test@{{.postgres.host}}:{{.postgres.port.5432}}/test"
    REDIS_URL: "redis://{{.redis.host}}:{{.redis.port.6379}}"

Port already in use

In command mode, tomato checks port before starting the app. If another process is already listening there (a local make run, a leftover test run), tomato fails instead of starting: otherwise the ready check would pass against the other process and the tests would hit the wrong app.

In command mode the app inherits tomato's environment, plus env. Some resources the app depends on while it starts are set up before it and add to that environment too: the aws resource points the app's AWS SDK at its STS and removes AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and friends inherited from your shell. The app's own env still wins over anything a resource sets.

The app runs in its own process group, and stopping it stops the whole group, so command: go run ./cmd/server (where go does not pass signals on) does not leave the server running and holding the port.

docs.title: Template variables
docs.text:
In app.env, you can use templates to inject container addresses:

Template Description {{.container_name.host}} Container hostname (localhost in command mode, the container's DNS name in container mode) {{.container_name.port.NNNN}} Host port that NNNN, the port inside the container, is mapped to {{.resource_name.url}} Base URL of an http-server resource

NNNN is required. A bare {{.container_name.port}} is left in the value verbatim, so the application receives the literal template text.

Example with PostgreSQL: 

containers:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15
    env:
      POSTGRES_USER: testuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
      POSTGRES_DB: testdb
    ports:
      - "5432"

app:
  command: ./my-app
  env:
    # These are resolved at runtime when containers start
    DB_HOST: "{{.postgres.host}}"
    DB_PORT: "{{.postgres.port.5432}}"
    DATABASE_URL: "postgres://testuser:testpass@{{.postgres.host}}:{{.postgres.port.5432}}/testdb"

Note: The container field in resource definitions automatically handles host/port resolution - you don't need to specify connection strings manually for resources.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
Define Docker containers for your test infrastructure.

containers:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15
    env:
      POSTGRES_USER: test
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
      POSTGRES_DB: test
    ports:
      - "5432"
    volumes:
      - ./init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql
    depends_on:
      - other_container
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "5432"
      timeout: 30s

volumes are source:target[:mode]. A source path (./x, ../x, /x, ~/x) is bound into the container, relative paths resolved against the directory of tomato.yml; a bare name is a Docker volume. build (context, dockerfile) builds the image instead of pulling one, with context relative to tomato.yml too. The image is named tomato-<container> and kept, so the next run rebuilds from cache into the same image. Each container's output is written to .tomato/runs/<run>/container-<name>.log for as long as it runs, including when it fails to start.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
A preset is a container tomato knows how to run. It fills in the image, env, ports and wait strategy; anything the entry sets itself (an env key, image, wait_for) wins.

containers:
  kafka:
    preset: kafka
    auth: aws_msk_iam   # optional: plaintext (default) or aws_msk_iam
Preset What it runs chromium A headless Chromium for browser resources. Pages it opens on localhost reach the app on your machine, through a tunnel to each port the suite uses there. See Browser. verapdf A veraPDF validation service for the pdf resource's conforms to step: PDF/UA and PDF/A, with the rules a document breaks in the failure. See PDF. kafka A single-node KRaft broker, reachable from the host and from other containers. With auth: aws_msk_iam, a second listener speaks SASL AWS_MSK_IAM like MSK's IAM port. See Kafka. redis A Redis server. With cluster: true it runs in cluster mode, one node owning every slot; with tls: true it speaks TLS only, with a certificate from a CA made for the run. Together, Redis the way ElastiCache runs it with cluster mode and in-transit encryption. See Redis.

docs.title: Resources tomato does not manage
docs.text:
tomato resets every resource before every scenario, and that is not configurable. A resource with no container: is a system tomato did not start, so resetting it destroys someone's real data. tomato refuses to load such a config:

resource "app-db" (postgres) has no container, so it points at a system tomato
does not manage — and tomato wipes every resource before every scenario,
which would destroy its data.

Give it a container: so tomato runs it, or, if it genuinely is a throwaway system, say so:

resources:
  app-db:
    type: postgres
    allow_destructive_reset: true   # yes, wipe it before every scenario
    options:
      host: scratch-db.internal

The acknowledgement stops the refusal, not the warning: tomato validate still flags it, and every run prints which unmanaged resources it is about to wipe. Only the stateful types are affected — postgres, redis, kafka, rabbitmq, s3, scylladb and their aliases. An http-client pointed at a remote URL holds no data, so it needs nothing.

docs.title: Container naming and reuse
docs.text:
Every container and network tomato creates is named and labelled, so docker ps says whose they are:

tomato-<project>-<run>-<container>     e.g. tomato-9a987f0c-06e8b19f-postgres
tomato-<project>-<run>-net             the network they share

<project> is derived from the config file's path, so two projects on one Docker host never collide; <run> is the run id, so two runs of the same project can go at once. Labels tomato.managed, tomato.scope, tomato.run and tomato.role are set on all of them, which is enough to find leftovers:

docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq --filter label=tomato.managed=true)
Setting Default Meaning settings.containers.reuse false Keep containers between runs instead of starting fresh ones

With reuse: true the run id drops out of the names, so a rerun finds what the last run left behind and skips container startup entirely. Resets still run before every scenario, so scenarios stay isolated from each other. What you give up: a container an earlier run corrupted is no longer thrown away, and two runs of the same project can no longer run at the same time. tomato leaves the containers running when the suite ends and prints the command to remove them.

docs.title: Wait strategies
docs.text: Type Description Fields port Wait for port to be ready target log Wait for log message target (regex) http Wait for HTTP endpoint path, target (port), method exec Run command in container target (command)

docs.title: Resetting state
docs.text:
Resetting is configured per resource, not per container — see options.reset_strategy under Resources and on each resource's page. How often it runs is not configurable: every resource is reset before every scenario. A scenario that needs a starting state builds it in a Background, which runs after the reset.

The opt-outs v2.3.0 removed, settings.reset, a resource's reset and reset_strategy: none, are refused at load with this explanation. A config written for an earlier release fails to load rather than having a resource it used to leave alone wiped before every scenario.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: Define handlers for test steps. The key is the name steps use to refer to the resource ("app-client" sends …), so it should say whose it is and what role it plays: orders-client, stripe-stub, orders-db, not api, mock or db. See Naming resources.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
resources:
  app-client:
    type: http
    base_url: http://localhost:8080
    options:
      timeout: 30s
Option Default Description timeout 30s Per-request timeout. For an event stream it bounds only the wait for the response headers; the stream stays open until the scenario closes it, and each receive step's within bounds its wait no_redirect false Return the redirect response instead of following it port 8080 Container port the base URL is built from. Only with container scheme http Scheme for the base URL built from container health_path (none) Path polled once at startup to check the service answers

Request headers are set by steps ("app-client" header "Authorization" is "..."), not here, and are cleared between scenarios.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
resources:
  app-db:
    type: postgres
    container: postgres
    database: test
    options:
      user: test
      password: test
      # Reset every table in these schemas (if neither this nor tables is set,
      # every table in public)
      schemas:
        - app
        - "plugin_*"       # any schema whose name matches
      # Reset these tables too
      tables:
        - public.outbox
      # Never truncate these tables (added to the defaults below)
      exclude:
        - countries        # reference data seeded by a migration

docs.title: Reset behavior
docs.text:
By default, PostgreSQL resources truncate all tables in the public schema before each scenario. You can control this behavior:

Option Description schemas Truncate every table in these schemas instead of public. A name containing * is a pattern tables Tables to truncate. Alone, only these are truncated; with schemas, these are truncated as well exclude Extra tables to never truncate, on top of the defaults: table in any schema, or schema.table

schemas is for an app that keeps its tables in more than one schema, a schema per module or per plugin, so the suite doesn't have to list every table and keep that list in step with the migrations. The tables are looked up in the catalog at every reset, so a table or a schema a migration adds is reset without a change to tomato.yml.

A schema named in schemas has to exist when the first scenario starts, which it does when the app creates it in its migrations at startup; otherwise the reset fails and says which schema is missing, rather than leaving its tables to leak state between scenarios. A pattern such as plugin_* may match no schema at all, since the schemas it stands for come and go: one a scenario creates is reset from the next scenario on. Quote a pattern in YAML.

Migration history tables are never truncated when the tables are found from a schema, in whichever schema they are, so migration tools still see their migrations as applied:

Tool Tables golang-migrate, Rails, sqlx schema_migrations goose goose_db_version Flyway flyway_schema_history Liquibase databasechangelog, databasechangeloglock

Reference data that migrations insert (countries, roles, permissions) is truncated like any other table. Add those tables to exclude so scenarios don't have to re-seed them.

A table listed in tables is always truncated, even when exclude or the list above names it. So when tables is set without schemas, exactly those tables are truncated, and both exclude and the migration-table list are ignored.

All the tables are truncated in one TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE statement, so a generated id starts again from 1 in every scenario.

The container field automatically provides the connection details - tomato resolves the container's host and port at runtime.

docs.title: ScyllaDB / Cassandra
docs.text:
resources:
  app-db:
    type: scylladb          # or: cassandra
    container: scylla
    options:
      keyspace: app         # created if missing, then used for unqualified tables
      schema:
        - ./fixtures/schema.cql
      exclude:
        - countries         # reference data kept across scenarios

Every table in the keyspace is truncated before each scenario, except those in exclude. See ScyllaDB Configuration for all options.

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
resources:
  app-cache:
    type: redis
    container: redis
    options:
      db: 0
      password: ""
      reset_strategy: flush  # flush or pattern
      reset_pattern: "*"     # For pattern strategy

docs.title: Kafka
docs.text:
resources:
  app-events:
    type: kafka
    container: kafka
    options:
      topics:
        - events
        - notifications
      partitions: 1
      replication_factor: 1
      reset_strategy: delete_recreate
      # Optional: Avro via Confluent Schema Registry
      schema_registry:
        container: schema-registry   # or url: http://localhost:8081
Field Default Description container — The container tomato starts and connects to brokers — Broker addresses, instead of container. A broker tomato does not start needs allow_destructive_reset: true, since its topics are recreated before every scenario

See Kafka: Avro and Schema Registry.

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
resources:
  app-ws-client:
    type: websocket
    url: ws://localhost:8080/ws
    # Or use container
    container: app
    options:
      port: "8080"
      path: /ws
      protocols:
        - graphql-ws
      headers:
        Authorization: Bearer token

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text:
resources:
  app-grpc-client:
    type: grpc
    address: "localhost:9090"   # or: container: myservice
    options:
      timeout: 30s

The server must register the gRPC reflection service. See gRPC Configuration.

docs.title: gRPC server
docs.text:
resources:
  users-stub:
    type: grpc-server
    options:
      port: 9995                              # fixed, so app.env can name it
      descriptor_set: proto/users.binpb       # buf build -o proto/users.binpb

app:
  env:
    USERS_ADDR: "{{.users-stub.address}}"     # localhost:9995

Stubs the gRPC services the app calls. See gRPC Server.

docs.title: S3
docs.text:
resources:
  uploads-storage:
    type: s3
    container: minio
    options:
      buckets:
        - uploads
      reset_strategy: purge   # purge or delete

See S3 Configuration for MinIO and LocalStack setup.

docs.title: Shell
docs.text:
resources:
  shell:
    type: shell
    options:
      timeout: 30s
      workdir: ./scripts
      env:
        PATH: /usr/local/bin

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Execute actions at different lifecycle points.

hooks:
  before_all:
    - sql_file: ./fixtures/schema.sql
      resource: app-db
    - shell: ./scripts/setup.sh

  after_all:
    - shell: ./scripts/cleanup.sh

  before_scenario:
    - sql: "DELETE FROM events"
      resource: app-db

  after_scenario:
    - exec: redis-cli FLUSHDB
      container: redis

docs.title: Hook types
docs.text: Type Description sql Execute SQL query sql_file Execute SQL file shell Run shell command exec Run command in container

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Configure feature file discovery.

features:
  paths:
    - ./features
    - ./integration/features
  tags: "@smoke and not @slow"

docs.title: Tag expressions
docs.text:
Expression Description @smoke Scenarios tagged with @smoke @smoke and @api Both tags @smoke or @api Either tag not @slow Exclude slow tests @smoke and not @wip Smoke tests, excluding WIP (@smoke or @api) and not @slow Parentheses group terms

not binds tighter than and, which binds tighter than or. godog's legacy syntax (@smoke && ~@slow, , for or) is still accepted.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Use environment variables anywhere in the config:

containers:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:${POSTGRES_VERSION}
    env:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}

Only $VAR and ${VAR} are expanded. Shell default syntax such as ${VAR:-15} is not supported: the whole VAR:-15 is read as the variable name, so the value expands to an empty string. Set the variable, or keep the default in tomato.yml.

docs.title: AWS configuration
docs.text:
The aws resource gives the application under test the AWS identity it gets on AWS through IRSA (IAM roles for service accounts): a role and a web identity token, which the application's AWS SDK exchanges at STS for session credentials. tomato serves that STS itself, so the application gets its credentials the way it does in production, and a test fails when that path breaks.

resources:
  aws:
    type: aws
    options:
      region: eu-central-1
      role_arn: arn:aws:iam::000000000000:role/my-service
      ambient_identity: true

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Description region us-east-1 Region the application is told it runs in role_arn arn:aws:iam::000000000000:role/tomato The IRSA role session_name tomato Role session name ambient_identity false Also leave a second, long-term identity where the SDK's credential chain looks after the role (see below) port random Port of the STS endpoint

docs.title: What the application gets
docs.text:
The resource starts before the application and adds to its environment:

Variable Value AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_ROLE_SESSION_NAME the role AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE a token file tomato writes AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_STS tomato's STS AWS_REGION, AWS_DEFAULT_REGION region AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE, AWS_CONFIG_FILE files tomato writes, so your own ~/.aws is never read AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED true

It also removes AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN, AWS_PROFILE and the container-credential variables from what the application inherits from your shell or CI, so credentials you happen to have never stand in for the role. The application's own env still wins. This applies to an application run as a local process (app.command).

The STS answers AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, AssumeRole and GetCallerIdentity. It does not verify tokens or signatures. The credentials it issues are stable per role, so a kafka preset with auth: aws_msk_iam knows to let exactly those in.

docs.title: The ambient identity
docs.text: On EKS, when an SDK cannot get the role's credentials, its credential chain keeps looking and can end up with another identity, such as the node's role. The service then authenticates as the wrong principal and is refused. ambient_identity: true puts such an identity in the shared credentials file, so that fallback happens in the test too, and ends the same way: an AWS_MSK_IAM listener that only admits the role's sessions answers Access denied.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The journal of assumed roles covers the whole run and is not reset between scenarios, because applications assume their role when they start. See AWS steps.

Then "aws" role "arn:aws:iam::000000000000:role/my-service" was assumed

docs.title: Browser configuration
docs.text:
The browser resource uses your application's web UI the way a person does, in a real headless Chromium: it opens pages, clicks and types into what it finds by the name a person reads — a button's label, a field's label, a paragraph's text — and asserts on what the page shows. The http resource sees the API; this one sees whether the UI shows the right thing and sends the right call when someone clicks.

version: 2

containers:
  chrome:
    preset: chromium

app:
  command: go run ./cmd/server
  port: 8080

resources:
  alice-browser:
    type: browser
    container: chrome
    options:
      base_url: http://localhost:8080
      viewport: 1440x900
      locale: de-DE
  bob-browser:
    type: browser
    container: chrome
    options:
      base_url: http://localhost:8080

Scenario: Two editors see each other's changes
  Given "alice-browser" opens "/master"
  And "bob-browser" opens "/master"
  When "alice-browser" types " Neuer Satz." at the end of "7.2"
  Then "bob-browser" sees "Neuer Satz." within "3s"

Each resource is its own browser context — its own cookies, local and session storage and service workers — in one shared Chromium, so two resources are two people. Collaboration needs no special syntax.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Meaning base_url none Where a path in opens "/master" is opened. 127.0.0.1 is read as localhost. Also accepted at the resource's top level, as for http. viewport 1280x720 The window size, WIDTHxHEIGHT. locale Chromium's The language the page sees: navigator.language, Intl formatting and the Accept-Language header of every request. screenshots .tomato/runs/<run>/screenshots Where screenshots are written. The default sits beside the run's logs, which CI keeps. timeout 5s How long a step waits for the element it names to appear, become enabled and stop being covered. port 9222 The DevTools port inside the container, for a container that is not the preset.

docs.title: How a step finds what it names
docs.text:
"alice-browser" clicks "Apply" does not take a CSS selector. tomato asks Chromium's accessibility tree for elements whose accessible name is Apply — the text of a button or link, the <label> of a field, aria-label, aria-labelledby, a placeholder — the same name a screen reader announces. When nothing has that name, the element whose visible text is exactly Apply is used. Only visible elements count.

  • Exactly one must match. When a button and a heading are both called Apply, the button wins: a person clicking Apply means the control. Two buttons called Delete fail the step and list both, rather than clicking whichever came first.
  • Every step waits up to timeout for the element to be there, enabled and not covered by something else (a modal's backdrop, a toast). After a click everything is asynchronous, so a step that fails on the first look would be a flaky step.
  • A click lands where it was aimed, or not at all. When the page moves between finding the element and the click arriving — a "Saving…" line appears above it, a banner slides in — the click would hit whatever moved under the pointer. tomato stops that click before the page sees it and tries again.
  • A label stands for its control. checks "Austria" finds the checkbox whether the text is in a <label> around it, a <label for> beside it or an aria-label on it. A checkbox styled away behind its label is clicked through the label, as a person would.
  • types "…" at the end of "7.2" finds the paragraph that shows 7.2 (the text may be part of a longer line), puts the caret after its last character, and types key by key: keydown, beforeinput, input, keyup. Rich-text editors such as ProseMirror and Tiptap see a person typing. fills replaces a field's content in one edit, as a paste would.

sees reads the page's rendered text (innerText) and the values of visible fields, with runs of whitespace as one space. Text in a hidden element, an attribute or the page's source is not seen, so does not see "clause_id" proves a structure the user must not see stays out of view.

sees and does not see assert the page now. After an action, wait for its outcome with sees "…" within "5s", or for something to go away with no longer sees "…" within "5s".

docs.title: The chromium preset
docs.text:
containers:
  chrome:
    preset: chromium

The preset runs chromedp/headless-shell (a pinned version), serves the DevTools protocol on port 9222, and waits until Chromium answers.

Reaching the app. The app runs on your machine, and inside a container localhost is the container. tomato does not rewrite URLs to another host name: that would change the page's origin, which breaks cookies, CORS, the absolute redirects an app builds, and the secure context browsers grant only to localhost over plain http (where crypto.randomUUID and service workers live). Instead, Chromium resolves the name localhost to your machine, through a tunnel testcontainers opens for each port the suite uses there: app.port, and every localhost port named by a browser, http or websocket resource's URL and by an http-server or websocket-server resource's port. The tunnel is an SSH connection from tomato to a small sidecar container (testcontainers/sshd), so it does not depend on host.docker.internal, which Docker on Linux and Lima do not point at the host.

Containers on tomato's network are reached by their name, as from any other container: base_url: http://frontend:3000.

Anything the entry sets as command is added to Chromium's flags:

containers:
  chrome:
    preset: chromium
    command: ["--force-prefers-reduced-motion"]

The preset's entrypoint relies on the layout of chromedp/headless-shell, so an image: override has to be another version of that image. To run a different browser image, leave the preset out and set image, ports: ["9222/tcp"] and wait_for yourself; localhost then means that container.

docs.title: Between scenarios
docs.text: Reset closes each person's browser context: its pages, cookies, storage and service workers. Chromium and its container keep running — a new context is cheap and a new browser is not — and the next step that needs a page opens a fresh one.

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
When a step fails, each person with an open page leaves a screenshot of what the page showed, named after the scenario and the resource, and the run's log says where it is:

INF screenshot of the page when the step failed path=.tomato/runs/…/screenshots/failed-Clause-structure-alice.png

It is attached to the failed step in the cucumber report too. To keep one from a passing scenario, "alice-browser" saves screenshot "after-apply" writes after-apply.png.

docs.title: Previewing them in tomato ui
docs.text: The inspector's Screenshots tab lists every screenshot the suite's browsers have written — each resource's screenshots directory, and the default places when the option is not set — newest first, with a thumbnail, when it was taken and its size. A click opens it at full size; esc closes it and the arrow keys step through the list. A step that saved a screenshot, or failed while a page was open, shows the picture on its own row, so the page a failure left behind is one click from the red step. The list follows the run: it refreshes as each step's picture lands, when the run ends, and when a screenshots directory changes.

docs.title: Dialogs
docs.text: alert(), confirm() and prompt() block a page until someone answers. The browser resource answers OK, as a person clicking through the flow would, and logs the dialog's message.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Elements inside an <iframe> are not found, and the visible-text fallback does not look inside shadow roots (the accessibility tree does).
  • A link that opens a new tab or window is not followed into it.
  • File uploads, downloads and drag and drop have no steps yet.
  • There is no step to narrow a lookup to part of the page ("Delete" in the row of order 42); give controls distinct accessible names, which helps screen-reader users as well.

docs.title: gRPC server configuration
docs.text: The grpc-server resource stands in for a gRPC service your application calls, the way http-server stands in for an HTTP one. A scenario stubs the methods it needs, the app calls them as it would the real service, and the scenario asserts on what the app sent.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
A stub has no server to ask for its schema over reflection, the way the grpc client does, so it is given one: a FileDescriptorSet, the compiled form of your .proto files. Either tool writes one:

buf build -o proto/users.binpb                       # imports included
protoc --include_imports --descriptor_set_out=proto/users.binpb users.proto

Commit it next to the suite, or build it in CI before tomato run. With protoc, --include_imports matters: a set missing an import fails with the file it is missing. The well-known types (google/protobuf/timestamp.proto and friends) are the exception; tomato has those built in.

Knowing the schema is what lets stubs and assertions be written as JSON, the same protojson the grpc client uses, and what makes a mistake fail at the step that makes it: a method that is not in the set fails with the ones that are, and a stubbed response with a misspelt field fails with the message type it did not fit.

docs.title: Resource configuration
docs.text:
resources:
  users-stub:
    type: grpc-server
    options:
      port: 9995
      descriptor_set: proto/users.binpb
Option Default Description descriptor_set — Required. Path to a FileDescriptorSet (.binpb, .pb), or a list of them. Relative to where tomato runs port 0 (a free port) Port to listen on. Fix it so app.env can name the address

The server speaks plaintext HTTP/2 (h2c), which is what a gRPC client dialing with insecure credentials expects. It serves every service in the set, and gRPC server reflection too, so grpcurl -plaintext localhost:9995 list and tomato's own grpc resource work against it.

It starts before the app does, so an app that dials or checks its dependencies while it starts finds it listening.

docs.title: Pointing your app at it
docs.text:
app.env names the server through its resource name:

app:
  command: go run ./cmd/server
  env:
    USERS_ADDR: "{{.users-stub.address}}"    # localhost:9995
    USERS_HOST: "{{.users-stub.host}}"       # localhost
    USERS_PORT: "{{.users-stub.port}}"       # 9995

A gRPC target is host:port, not a URL, so the address is the usual one to use. With the app in a container, the host is host.docker.internal. Templates need a fixed port; without one they are left as they are.

docs.title: Stubbing
docs.text:
Scenario: The page shows the user's name
  Given "users-stub" stub "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" returns json:
    """
    {"id": "42", "name": "Alice", "role": "ROLE_ADMIN"}
    """
  When "app-client" sends "GET" to "/profile/42"
  Then "app-client" response json "name" is "Alice"

The docstring is the response message in protojson: field names in lowerCamelCase (or as in the .proto), enums by name, Timestamp as an RFC 3339 string.

A failure is a status, with an optional message:

Given "users-stub" stub "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" returns status "NOT_FOUND" with message "no user 42"

Status names follow the gRPC spec (NOT_FOUND, PERMISSION_DENIED, UNAVAILABLE, ...); grpc-go's NotFound and the number work too.

docs.title: Which calls a stub answers
docs.text:
Between the method and returns, conditions narrow the calls a stub answers:

  • with metadata "authorization" "Bearer {{token}}": a metadata value, exactly.
  • with request json "id" "42": a field of the request message. The path is the one JSON assertions use (user.address.city, items[0].sku), and the value takes the same @ matchers: "@startswith:secret-", "@gt:10".
Given "users-stub" stub "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" returns json:
  """
  {"id": "1", "name": "Bob"}
  """
And "users-stub" stub "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" with request json "id" "404" returns status "NOT_FOUND"

The most specific stub wins, then the most recent, so a scenario can override what its Background stubbed. A call no stub answers gets UNIMPLEMENTED, with a message naming the method and, when stubs for it exist, what they need.

docs.title: Over several calls, and slowly
docs.text:
returns in sequence: answers each call with the next row and repeats the last one. A row is a message (json) or a failure (status, message), and delay answers late:

Given "users-stub" stub "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" returns in sequence:
  | status      | message    | json                          | delay |
  | UNAVAILABLE | warming up |                               |       |
  | OK          |            | {"id": "42", "name": "Slow"}  | 3s    |
  | OK          |            | {"id": "42", "name": "Alice"} |       |

A delay respects the caller's deadline: an app that gives the call one second gets DEADLINE_EXCEEDED after one second, and the stub stops waiting.

docs.title: Server streaming
docs.text:
streams: answers a server-streaming method with one message per row, then ends the stream. A last row with a status ends it with that status instead:

Given "users-stub" stub "users.v1.UserService/WatchUsers" streams:
  | json                         | delay | status      | message          |
  | {"id": "1", "name": "Alice"} |       |             |                  |
  | {"id": "2", "name": "Bob"}   | 50ms  |             |                  |
  |                              |       | UNAVAILABLE | connection reset |

returns json: on a streaming method sends a stream of one message.

docs.title: Asserting on what the app sent
docs.text:
Then "users-stub" received "users.v1.UserService/GetUser"
And "users-stub" received "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" "2" times
And "users-stub" did not receive "users.v1.UserService/DeleteUser"
And "users-stub" received "3" calls
And "users-stub" received "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" with metadata "authorization" "Bearer {{token}}"
And "users-stub" last "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" request metadata "authorization" is "Bearer {{token}}"
And "users-stub" last "users.v1.UserService/ListUsers" request json contains:
  """
  {"pageSize": 50}
  """

The request is rendered as JSON with its zero values, like the grpc client's responses, so a field that is 0, "" or false is there to assert on. A value the app generated can be kept for later steps:

And "users-stub" last "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" request json "id" saved as "{{user_id}}"
And "users-stub" last "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" request metadata "x-request-id" saved as "{{request_id}}"

Metadata keys are case-insensitive, as gRPC sends them in lower case.

docs.title: The service is down
docs.text:
Given "users-stub" refuses connections
When "app-client" sends "GET" to "/profile/42"
Then "app-client" response status is "503"
When "users-stub" accepts connections

refuses connections closes the port and the connections the app already has open, so its calls fail with UNAVAILABLE; calls in flight finish first. accepts connections opens it again on the same address, with the stubs kept. A gRPC client backs off before reconnecting, so the app's first call after that may still fail, depending on its channel settings.

docs.title: Reset behavior
docs.text: Before every scenario the stubs and the recorded calls are cleared, and a server left refusing connections accepts them again.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
version: 2

app:
  command: go run ./cmd/server
  port: 8080
  ready:
    type: http
    path: /health
  env:
    USERS_ADDR: "{{.users-stub.address}}"

resources:
  app-client:
    type: http-client
    base_url: http://localhost:8080
  users-stub:
    type: grpc-server
    options:
      port: 9995
      descriptor_set: proto/users.binpb

Feature: Profile page

  Scenario: The user's token reaches the user service
    Given "users-stub" stub "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" with metadata "authorization" "Bearer alice" returns json:
      """
      {"id": "42", "name": "Alice"}
      """
    And "app-client" header "Authorization" is "Bearer alice"
    When "app-client" sends "GET" to "/profile/42"
    Then "app-client" response status is "200"
    And "users-stub" last "users.v1.UserService/GetUser" request json contains:
      """
      {"id": "42"}
      """

See gRPC Server Steps for every step.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Unary and server-streaming methods only. A client-streaming or bidirectional method cannot be stubbed yet: the step says so, and a call to one is recorded and answered UNIMPLEMENTED. Stubbing those needs steps for what arrives over time, which is a design of its own.
  • No response metadata or trailers on stubbed answers yet.
  • Plaintext only: no TLS.
  • No .proto files directly. Build a descriptor set from them with buf or protoc.

docs.title: gRPC configuration
docs.text:
The grpc resource calls unary gRPC methods and asserts on what comes back. To stand in for a gRPC service your application calls, use gRPC Server instead.

Methods are resolved through server reflection, so you name a method the way you would say it out loud — helloworld.Greeter/SayHello — and no .proto file or generated stub has to live next to your tests. The server already knows its own schema; a second copy beside the suite is a copy that goes stale.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
The server under test must register the reflection service. This is the one hard requirement, and it is checked at startup so a server without it fails with an explanation rather than at your first call step.

In Go:

import "google.golang.org/grpc/reflection"

srv := grpc.NewServer()
pb.RegisterYourServiceServer(srv, impl)
reflection.Register(srv)   // <- this

Both the stable v1 reflection API and the older v1alpha are supported; tomato prefers v1 and falls back automatically, so servers that predate the stable API — grpc-java's ProtoReflectionService, for instance — work unchanged.

docs.title: Connecting to a fixed address
docs.text:
resources:
  greeter-client:
    type: grpc
    address: "localhost:9090"

address is a dial target (host:port), not a URL — no scheme.

docs.title: Connecting to a managed container
docs.text:
containers:
  myservice:
    image: myorg/myservice:latest
    ports:
      - "9090/tcp"
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "9090"

resources:
  greeter-client:
    type: grpc
    container: myservice
    options:
      port: "9090"      # container port to map; defaults to 9090

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Description address — Dial target host:port. Either this or container is required. container — Managed container to dial instead of a fixed address. options.port 9090 Container port to map. Only used with container. options.timeout 30s Per-call deadline, also used for reflection lookups. options.tls false Dial with TLS using the system roots. Plaintext otherwise.

docs.title: Writing requests and reading responses
docs.text:
Request and response messages are JSON, converted with protojson:

When "greeter-client" calls "helloworld.Greeter/SayHello" with:
  """
  {"name": "tomato"}
  """
Then "greeter-client" call succeeds
And "greeter-client" response json "message" is "Hello tomato"

Because the response is rendered as JSON, every JSON assertion tomato already has works against a protobuf message — paths, matches, contains and the full matcher vocabulary (@notempty, @regex:..., @gt:n, …).

Two conversion details worth knowing:

  • Enums render as their names, so assert "SERVING", not 2.
  • Zero values are emitted. A field that is legitimately 0, "" or false still appears in the response, so asserting on it reads as "the value is zero" rather than "the path does not exist".

docs.title: Asserting on failures
docs.text:
A non-OK status is a result, not an error. The call step records it and lets you assert on it, because "this request is rejected" is a normal thing to test:

When "greeter-client" calls "helloworld.Greeter/SayHello" with:
  """
  {"name": ""}
  """
Then "greeter-client" call fails
And "greeter-client" response status is "INVALID_ARGUMENT"
And "greeter-client" response error contains "name is required"

Status names are matched ignoring case and underscores, so INVALID_ARGUMENT, InvalidArgument and the number 3 all work.

Only a problem with the call itself — an unknown method, or a request that is not valid for the schema — fails the step. Those errors are specific: an unknown method lists the methods that do exist, and an invalid request names the message type it failed to parse into.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Given "greeter-client" metadata "authorization" is "Bearer {{token}}"
And "greeter-client" metadata are:
  | key          | value   |
  | x-request-id | abc-123 |

A key/value header row is skipped, so tables can be written either way.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: Unary calls only. Streaming needs its own vocabulary for opening a stream, sending over time and asserting on a sequence — that is a different design rather than more steps on this one. A streaming method is refused with a clear message rather than attempted.

docs.title: HTTP server configuration
docs.text: This guide covers how to configure the HTTP Server handler for mocking external services in integration tests.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The HTTP Server handler creates a local mock server that can stub HTTP endpoints. This is useful for testing how your application interacts with external APIs without actually calling them.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Mock third-party APIs (payment gateways, notification services, etc.)
  • Simulate various response scenarios (success, errors, timeouts)
  • Verify your application sends correct requests
  • Test retry logic and error handling

docs.title: Resource configuration
docs.text:
The HTTP Server is a standalone handler that doesn't require a container:

resources:
  payments-stub:
    type: http-server
    options:
      port: 9999

docs.title: Resource options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description port int 0 (random) Port to listen on. Use 0 for system-assigned port, or specify a fixed port

docs.title: Configuring your app to use mock servers
docs.text:
Since your application needs to call the mock server instead of the real external API, you must configure the mock server URLs via environment variables.

Use the {{.resource_name.url}} template syntax to reference mock server URLs:

resources:
  payments-stub:
    type: http-server
    options:
      port: 9001

  notifications-stub:
    type: http-server
    options:
      port: 9002

app:
  command: go run ./cmd/server
  env:
    # Use template syntax to reference mock server URLs
    PAYMENT_API_URL: "{{.payments-stub.url}}"
    NOTIFICATION_API_URL: "{{.notifications-stub.url}}"

The templates resolve to: - Command mode: http://localhost:{port} (e.g., http://localhost:9001) - Container mode: http://host.docker.internal:{port} (accessible from Docker)

Your application code should read these URLs from environment variables:

paymentAPIURL := os.Getenv("PAYMENT_API_URL")
// Use paymentAPIURL when making HTTP calls to payment service

Fixed Ports Required

HTTP server resources must have a fixed port configured in options for the URL template to work. Without a port, the template cannot be resolved.

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
Here's a complete tomato.yml with multiple mock servers:

version: 2

settings:
  timeout: 5m
  fail_fast: false
  output: pretty

resources:
  # Mock external payment gateway
  payments-stub:
    type: http-server
    options:
      port: 9001

  # Mock notification service
  notifications-stub:
    type: http-server
    options:
      port: 9002

  # HTTP client to test your app
  app-client:
    type: http-client
    base_url: "http://localhost:8080"

app:
  command: go run ./cmd/server
  port: 8080
  env:
    # Templates resolve to http://localhost:9001, http://localhost:9002
    PAYMENT_API_URL: "{{.payments-stub.url}}"
    NOTIFICATION_API_URL: "{{.notifications-stub.url}}"
  ready:
    type: http
    path: /health
    timeout: 30s

features:
  paths:
    - ./features

docs.title: Basic stubbing
docs.text:
Feature: Payment Processing

  Scenario: Process successful payment
    # Stub the payment gateway
    Given "payments-stub" stub "POST" "/charge" returns "200" with json:
      """
      {"transaction_id": "txn_123", "status": "success"}
      """
    # Your app calls the payment gateway
    When "app-client" sends "POST" to "/process-payment" with json:
      """
      {"amount": 100, "currency": "USD"}
      """
    Then "app-client" response status is "200"
    And "app-client" response json "status" is "completed"

docs.title: Stubbing different responses
docs.text:
Scenario: Handle payment gateway error
  Given "payments-stub" stub "POST" "/charge" returns "500" with json:
    """
    {"error": "Gateway unavailable"}
    """
  When "app-client" sends "POST" to "/process-payment" with json:
    """
    {"amount": 100}
    """
  Then "app-client" response status is "503"

docs.title: Custom response headers
docs.text:
Scenario: API returns rate limit headers
  Given "payments-stub" stub "GET" "/balance" returns "200" with headers:
    | header           | value |
    | X-RateLimit-Remaining | 99    |
    | X-RateLimit-Reset     | 3600  |
  When "app-client" sends "GET" to "/check-balance"
  Then "app-client" response status is "200"

docs.title: Verifying requests
docs.text:
Scenario: Verify authorization header is sent
  Given "payments-stub" stub "POST" "/charge" returns "200"
  When "app-client" sends "POST" to "/process-payment" with json:
    """
    {"amount": 50}
    """
  Then "payments-stub" received "POST" "/charge"
  And "payments-stub" received request with header "Authorization" containing "Bearer"

Scenario: Verify request body
  Given "payments-stub" stub "POST" "/charge" returns "200"
  When "app-client" sends "POST" to "/process-payment" with json:
    """
    {"amount": 75, "currency": "EUR"}
    """
  Then "payments-stub" received request with body containing "EUR"

docs.title: Request counting
docs.text:
Scenario: Verify retry behavior
  # Stub fails first two times, succeeds third
  Given "payments-stub" stub "POST" "/charge" returns "503"
  When "app-client" sends "POST" to "/process-payment-with-retry"
  # App should have retried 3 times
  Then "payments-stub" received "POST" "/charge" "3" times

docs.title: Negative assertions
docs.text:
Scenario: Verify no unauthorized calls
  Given "payments-stub" stub "GET" "/balance" returns "200"
  When "app-client" sends "GET" to "/public-info"
  Then "payments-stub" did not receive "GET" "/balance"

See HTTP Server Steps for the complete list of available steps.

docs.title: Multiple mock servers
docs.text:
You can configure multiple mock servers for different external services:

resources:
  payments-stub:
    type: http-server
    options:
      port: 9001

  notifications-stub:
    type: http-server
    options:
      port: 9002

  analytics-stub:
    type: http-server
    options:
      port: 9003

docs.title: Reset behavior
docs.text:
Between each scenario: - All stubs are cleared - All recorded calls are cleared

This ensures each scenario starts with a clean slate.

docs.title: Port already in use
docs.text:
If you get "address already in use" error:

  1. Use port: 0 to let the system assign a free port
  2. Or kill processes using the specified port: lsof -ti:9999 | xargs kill -9

docs.title: Requests not being recorded
docs.text:
1. Verify the URL in your test matches the stub path exactly
  2. Check that the HTTP method matches (GET vs POST)
  3. Ensure your application is pointing to the mock server's port

docs.title: Stub not matching
docs.text: Stubs match in order they were defined. If a request doesn't match any stub, the server returns 404 with a message indicating no stub was found.

docs.title: Kafka configuration
docs.text: This guide covers how to configure Apache Kafka for integration testing with tomato.

docs.title: Preset
docs.text:
The shortest setup is the kafka preset. tomato picks the host port, advertises it, and points the kafka resource at it:

containers:
  kafka:
    preset: kafka

resources:
  orders-events:
    type: kafka
    container: kafka
    options:
      topics: [orders]

It is a single-node KRaft broker with these listeners:

Listener For Address plain the host: tomato, an app run as a local process {{.kafka.host}}:{{.kafka.port.9092}} plain other containers on tomato's network kafka:29092 AWS_MSK_IAM (auth: aws_msk_iam) the host {{.kafka.host}}:{{.kafka.port.9098}} AWS_MSK_IAM (auth: aws_msk_iam) other containers kafka:29098

The kafka resource always uses the plain listener.

docs.title: MSK IAM authentication
docs.text:
auth: aws_msk_iam adds a listener that speaks SASL AWS_MSK_IAM, the mechanism aws-msk-iam-auth uses against MSK. Point the app at it with the same client settings it uses in production, SASL_PLAINTEXT in place of SASL_SSL:

containers:
  kafka:
    preset: kafka
    auth: aws_msk_iam

resources:
  aws:
    type: aws
    options:
      role_arn: arn:aws:iam::000000000000:role/my-service

app:
  command: java -jar build/libs/my-service.jar
  env:
    SPRING_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: "{{.kafka.host}}:{{.kafka.port.9098}}"
    SPRING_KAFKA_PROPERTIES_SECURITY_PROTOCOL: SASL_PLAINTEXT
    SPRING_KAFKA_PROPERTIES_SASL_MECHANISM: AWS_MSK_IAM
    SPRING_KAFKA_PROPERTIES_SASL_JAAS_CONFIG: "software.amazon.msk.auth.iam.IAMLoginModule required;"
    SPRING_KAFKA_PROPERTIES_SASL_CLIENT_CALLBACK_HANDLER_CLASS: software.amazon.msk.auth.iam.IAMClientCallbackHandler

The listener checks who the client is, not its signature. With an aws resource in the config it lets in only the role sessions that resource's STS issues, and tells any other identity Access denied, as MSK does for a role without the kafka-cluster policy. So an app that ends up with the wrong credentials (its SDK could not reach STS and fell back to another identity, say) fails here the way it fails against MSK. Without an aws resource, any identity gets in.

docs.title: The image
docs.text: The preset runs the stock apache/kafka:3.9.1. For auth: aws_msk_iam, tomato copies the AWS_MSK_IAM server it carries in its binary into the container's /opt/kafka/libs before the broker starts, so there is no extra image to pull or build. Set image: on the entry to run another apache/kafka tag; the plugin is copied into it the same way.

docs.title: Manual setup without the preset
docs.text: Reach for this only when you need a broker the preset does not cover — a different distribution, or a Zookeeper-based cluster to match production. Otherwise use preset: kafka above; it is what tomato's own integration suite runs.

docs.title: Why a broker needs extra configuration
docs.text: Kafka's advertised listeners are fixed at startup, before Docker assigns a dynamic host port, so a client on the host cannot discover the mapped port. The way around it is a fixed port mapping for the external listener plus a second listener for traffic between containers. The preset does this for you.

docs.title: Container setup
docs.text:
Zookeeper with Kafka and dual listeners:

containers:
  zookeeper:
    image: confluentinc/cp-zookeeper:7.6.1
    env:
      ZOOKEEPER_CLIENT_PORT: "2181"
      ZOOKEEPER_TICK_TIME: "2000"
    ports:
      - "2181/tcp"
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "2181/tcp"
      timeout: 30s

  kafka:
    image: confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.1
    depends_on:
      - zookeeper
    env:
      KAFKA_BROKER_ID: "1"
      KAFKA_ZOOKEEPER_CONNECT: "{{.zookeeper.host}}:{{.zookeeper.port.2181}}"
      # Dual listeners: internal (kafka:29092) and external (localhost:9092)
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:29092,PLAINTEXT_HOST://localhost:9092
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT_HOST:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: "1"
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: "0"
      KAFKA_AUTO_CREATE_TOPICS_ENABLE: "true"
    ports:
      # Fixed port for external access (host connects here)
      - "9092:9092"
      # Internal port for container-to-container (dynamic is fine)
      - "29092/tcp"
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "9092/tcp"
      timeout: 60s

docs.title: Dual listeners
docs.text:
Kafka is configured with two listeners:

Listener Address Purpose PLAINTEXT kafka:29092 Internal communication between containers PLAINTEXT_HOST localhost:9092 External access from host machine (tests)

docs.title: Fixed port mapping
docs.text:
The external port uses fixed mapping (9092:9092) so the advertised listener (localhost:9092) matches the actual port:

ports:
  - "9092:9092"    # Fixed: host:container
  - "29092/tcp"    # Dynamic: just container port

docs.title: Environment variable templates
docs.text:
Tomato supports templates in container environment variables:

Template Resolves To {{.container_name.host}} Container's DNS name (for inter-container communication) {{.container_name.port.XXXX}} Container's internal port (not mapped host port)

For Zookeeper connection: 

KAFKA_ZOOKEEPER_CONNECT: "{{.zookeeper.host}}:{{.zookeeper.port.2181}}"

This resolves to zookeeper:2181 (container DNS name + internal port).

docs.title: Resource configuration
docs.text:
Configure the Kafka resource to connect to the container:

resources:
  orders-events:
    type: kafka
    container: kafka
    options:
      topics:
        - orders
        - events
        - notifications
      partitions: 1
      replication_factor: 1
      reset_strategy: delete_recreate

docs.title: Resource options
docs.text: Option Type Description topics list Topics to create/manage partitions int Number of partitions per topic (default: 1) replication_factor int Replication factor (default: 1) reset_strategy string How to reset between scenarios

docs.title: Reset strategies
docs.text: Strategy Description delete_recreate Delete and recreate topics (recommended) none No reset between scenarios

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
A complete tomato.yml with Kafka, using the preset:

version: 2

settings:
  timeout: 5m
  fail_fast: false
  output: pretty

containers:
  kafka:
    preset: kafka

resources:
  orders-events:
    type: kafka
    container: kafka
    options:
      topics:
        - user-events
        - order-events
      partitions: 1
      replication_factor: 1
      reset_strategy: delete_recreate

features:
  paths:
    - ./features

docs.title: Writing Kafka tests
docs.text:
Once configured, you can write Gherkin scenarios to test Kafka:

Feature: Event Processing

  Scenario: Order events are published correctly
    Given "orders-events" creates topic "order-events"
    And "orders-events" consumes from "order-events"
    When "orders-events" publishes json to "order-events" with key "order-123":
      """
      {"event": "order.created", "orderId": "123", "amount": 99.99}
      """
    Then "orders-events" receives from "order-events" with key "order-123" within "10s"
    And "orders-events" last message contains:
      """
      order.created
      """

See Kafka Steps for the complete list of available steps.

docs.title: Avro and Schema Registry
docs.text: Tomato speaks the Confluent wire format: a magic byte, a 4-byte schema id, then the Avro body. That is what KafkaAvroSerializer and KafkaAvroDeserializer read and write, so a JVM app under test sees ordinary Avro messages. Feature files stay plain JSON.

docs.title: Add a schema registry
docs.text:
containers:
  schema-registry:
    image: confluentinc/cp-schema-registry:7.6.1
    depends_on:
      - kafka
    env:
      SCHEMA_REGISTRY_HOST_NAME: schema-registry
      SCHEMA_REGISTRY_LISTENERS: http://0.0.0.0:8081
      SCHEMA_REGISTRY_KAFKASTORE_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:29092
    ports:
      - "8081/tcp"
    wait_for:
      type: http
      path: /subjects
      target: "8081"
      timeout: 90s

resources:
  orders-events:
    type: kafka
    container: kafka
    options:
      topics: [orders]
      schema_registry:
        container: schema-registry     # or: url: http://localhost:8081
        subjects:                      # optional, topic -> subject
          payments: com.example.Payment

app:
  env:
    SPRING_KAFKA_PROPERTIES_SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL: "http://{{.schema-registry.host}}:{{.schema-registry.port.8081}}"
Option Description schema_registry.url Registry base URL schema_registry.container Container running the registry; tomato resolves host and mapped port schema_registry.port Registry port inside the container (default 8081) schema_registry.subjects Map a topic to a subject. Default is <topic>-value (TopicNameStrategy)

docs.title: Writing Avro tests
docs.text:
Scenario: Order service emits an OrderCreated event
  Given "orders-events" registers schema for subject "orders-value" from file "schemas/order.avsc"
  And "orders-events" consumes from "orders"
  When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
    """
    {"id": "order-1", "amount": 4200}
    """
  Then "orders-events" receives avro from "orders" within "10s":
    """
    {"id": "order-1", "status": "CREATED"}
    """
  And "orders-events" last message avro matches:
    """
    {"id": "order-1", "amount": 4200, "status": "CREATED", "note": null}
    """
  • publishes avro to "topic" encodes the JSON with the latest schema of the topic's value subject. Register it first, or let the app register it.
  • receives avro from ... within waits for a message whose decoded JSON contains the given fields, so other messages on the topic don't break the test. last message avro matches compares the whole record exactly.
  • Nullable fields (["null", "string"]) are written as plain JSON values ("rush" or null), not Avro-JSON's {"string": "rush"}.
  • Keys are sent and asserted as strings. Avro keys, schema references and Protobuf/JSON Schema subjects are not supported yet.

docs.title: AWS Glue Schema Registry
docs.text:
An app that uses the AWS Glue Schema Registry writes and reads a different wire format, and resolves schemas by calling Glue through the AWS SDK. With format: glue, tomato speaks that format and serves the Glue API itself, so the app fetches the schema the scenario registered and no AWS account is involved:

resources:
  trades-events:
    type: kafka
    container: kafka
    options:
      topics: [trade-events]
      schema_registry:
        format: glue
        registry_name: portfolio   # default: default-registry
        region: eu-central-1       # in the schema ARNs; default us-east-1
        compression: zlib          # how tomato writes values: none (default) or zlib
        port: 9994                 # of the Glue endpoint; default: a free port
Option Default Description format confluent glue for the AWS Glue Schema Registry registry_name default-registry The registry schemas are registered in and looked up from region us-east-1 Region in the schema ARNs the API returns compression none zlib compresses the values tomato publishes. Values the app publishes are read either way port free port Port of the Glue endpoint

Wire format. [0x03][0x00 none | 0x05 zlib][16-byte schema version UUID][Avro binary].

The app is pointed at it. The resource sets AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_GLUE in the app's environment, so the AWS SDK sends Glue calls to tomato. Pair it with the aws resource for the credentials those calls are signed with; tomato does not verify signatures. The endpoint answers GetSchemaVersion, GetSchemaByDefinition, CreateSchema, RegisterSchemaVersion and GetSchema, the operations the AWS Glue SerDe calls. Anything else gets an UnsupportedOperationException that names it.

Subjects are schema names. The steps are the same as for the Confluent registry; a topic's schema is named after the topic (the SerDe's default), unless subjects maps it:

Given "trades-events" registers schema for subject "trade-events" from file "schemas/trade.avsc"
When "trades-events" publishes avro to "trade-events" with key "user-1":
  """
  {"tradeId": "t-1", "quantity": "10"}
  """

Registered schemas last for the whole run, as in a real registry: the app caches schemas by version id. Registering a definition that is already a version of the schema, in any layout, returns that version.

docs.title: Connection refused
docs.text:
If tests fail with "connection refused":

  1. Verify Kafka container is healthy: docker ps
  2. Check the broker's port is mapped: docker port <container_id>
  3. With the manual setup, make sure nothing else holds port 9092: lsof -i :9092

docs.title: Consumer not receiving messages
docs.text:
1. Ensure consumes from is called before publishing
  2. The consumer starts at OffsetNewest - only messages published after consumer starts are received
  3. Verify topic exists with topic "name" exists

docs.title: Port already in use
docs.text:
The manual setup pins the external listener to 9092:9092, so a second Kafka on that port clashes. The preset picks a free host port and is unaffected.

# Kill any process using port 9092
lsof -ti:9092 | xargs kill -9

docs.title: Lifecycle configuration
docs.text:
The lifecycle resource takes the application or one of its dependencies down in the middle of a scenario, the way production fails: the app restarts under connected clients, a database restarts, a broker hangs. The scenario then drives the app and checks that it recovers.

resources:
  lifecycle:
    type: lifecycle

It has no options. The steps name the containers from containers: in tomato.yml.

Scenario: The app keeps its orders across a database failover
  Given "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
    """
    {"id": "o-1"}
    """
  When "lifecycle" restarts container "postgres"
  And "orders-client" sends "GET" to "/orders/o-1"
  Then "orders-client" response status is "200"

docs.title: What each step does
docs.text: Step Production failure What tomato does restarts the app a deploy or a crash stops the app process and starts it again, waiting for its ready check restarts the app with env: a changed setting the same, with these variables changed for the rest of the scenario stops the app / starts the app the app is down for a while stops it, and later starts it and waits for its ready check stops container / starts container a dependency goes down stops the container, keeping its data, and starts it again on the same host port restarts container a failover stop, then start pauses container / unpauses container a hung dependency, a network partition freezes its processes: connections stay open and nothing answers

docs.title: Every scenario starts with everything up
docs.text: Before each scenario, the lifecycle resource starts the containers the last scenario stopped, unpauses the ones it paused, and restarts the app with its configured environment if the scenario stopped it or changed its environment. This runs before any other resource resets, so a postgres reset never meets a stopped database.

docs.title: Same address after a restart
docs.text: Docker gives a container a new host port every time it starts, so a database that stops and starts would come back where the app no longer looks. With a local Docker, tomato binds each dynamic container port to a free host port it picks itself, and the container keeps that address for the whole run. A remote Docker host (DOCKER_HOST=tcp://...) keeps Docker's own allocation.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Stopping and starting the app needs app.command: an app run as a container is removed when it stops and comes back on another port.
  • Data a container keeps in memory only (Redis without persistence, say) is gone after a restart, as it would be in production.

docs.title: Network configuration
docs.text:
The network resource puts a proxy between the application and one of the containers it depends on, so a scenario can make that dependency slow, cut its connections, make it hang or refuse connections, and then check what the application does: whether it times out, retries, reconnects, or answers its own callers sensibly.

It works on TCP, so it works the same for every dependency in a container: Postgres, Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ, ScyllaDB, MinIO and anything else.

containers:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    ports: ["5432/tcp"]

app:
  command: ./orders
  env:
    DATABASE_URL: "postgres://test:test@{{.postgres.host}}:{{.postgres.port.5432}}/test?sslmode=disable"

resources:
  orders-db:
    type: postgres
    container: postgres

  postgres-network:
    type: network
    container: postgres

Scenario: an order survives a database failover
  Given "postgres-network" resets connections for "3s"
  When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
    """
    {"id": "ord-1", "total": 1999}
    """
  Then "orders-client" response status is "201"
  And "orders-db" table "orders" has "1" rows

docs.title: Only the application goes through it
docs.text:
With a network resource in front of postgres, the application's {{.postgres.port.5432}} resolves to the proxy, and every connection it opens goes through it. tomato's own resources, orders-db above, still connect to the container directly, so the steps that check a result are never slowed down or cut off by the faults a scenario applies.

At the start of a run tomato prints where each proxy listens:

  ⇄ postgres-network  app → 127.0.0.1:51726 → postgres:5432  (seed 42)

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Description ports every port the container exposes The container ports to stand in front of, like [5432] seed random, printed at the start of the run Decides which connections fails "30%" of new connections fails, so a failing run can be repeated with the same seed

docs.title: Faults
docs.text:
Every fault lasts until the scenario ends or the network is healed. Each one also takes for "<duration>", after which it heals by itself, which is what retry and reconnect code has to survive.

Step What the application sees adds latency "300ms" every response 300 ms late; with jitter "100ms" varies it limits bandwidth to "64KB/s" a slow link stops responding a hung dependency: requests are accepted and never answered, until its own timeout resets connections every connection reset (TCP RST) as soon as it carries data, as in a crash or failover refuses connections open connections closed and new ones refused, as when the dependency is down; the container keeps running and keeps its data flaps every "2s" down and up in turn fails the next "2" connections the next two new connections closed as soon as they open; the ones already open are untouched fails "30%" of new connections a seeded share of new connections closed as soon as they open loses "30%" of the data chunks of the stream dropped: stalls and a garbled protocol, not TCP packet loss, which TCP would repair is healthy every fault turned off

Faults apply to connections that are already open, such as a connection pool's, as well as to new ones.

docs.title: Checking what the application did
docs.text:
Step Checks has seen "3" connections how many connections the application opened since the scenario started, failed ones included; a retry or a reconnect is a new one sees a new connection within "10s" that the application opened a connection after the network last changed: it reconnected 
Scenario: the worker reconnects after the broker drops it
  Given "rabbitmq-network" resets connections for "2s"
  Then "rabbitmq-network" sees a new connection within "15s"

docs.title: Every scenario starts on a healthy network
docs.text: Before every scenario the resource turns every fault off and forgets the connections it counted. It does so before the other resources reset, so postgres truncates its tables and kafka recreates its topics over a healthy link.

docs.title: In the reports
docs.text:
A step that fails while a fault is on says so, after its own error, in every output format:

expected status 200, got 502
while the network was faulty:
  minio-network resets connections (step 3, 5s left)
  minio-network has seen 1 connection this scenario, 0 failed
  postgres-network adds latency 300ms (step 2)

The connection count appears once the network has seen a connection.

The tomato event stream, which tomato ui reads, carries on each step_end what the network resources did while the step ran, with timestamps, and the faults that were on. In tomato ui, a step that ran on a faulty network has a band and a badge naming the networks (hover it for the faults), and the step during which a fault was applied, healed or failed a connection lists it with the time:

docs.title: Kafka
docs.text:
A Kafka client dials the bootstrap address once and then the address the broker advertises, so a proxy in front of the bootstrap port alone would be bypassed after the first request. With the kafka preset, tomato takes care of it: the broker advertises the proxy to the application, on the plain listener and the AWS_MSK_IAM one, and a listener of its own to tomato's kafka resource.

containers:
  kafka:
    preset: kafka

resources:
  orders-events:
    type: kafka
    container: kafka
  kafka-network:
    type: network
    container: kafka

A broker configured by hand has to advertise the proxy itself.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The application runs as a local process (app.command). In container mode it reaches its dependencies over the Docker network, past a proxy in tomato's process, so tomato refuses the combination at the start of a run.
  • TCP, blind to the protocol. A fault applies to every connection to the container, so it cannot fail only the INSERTs or one Kafka topic. For HTTP and gRPC dependencies, the HTTP server and gRPC server stubs answer late or fail per request.
  • One network resource per container.
