The design, and a spike that tried every fault against Postgres, Redis, MinIO, RabbitMQ and Kafka clients, is in Design: network faults.

docs.title: PDF configuration
docs.text:
The pdf resource asserts on what is inside the PDF documents your application generates: the page count, the text (on the document, on one page, and the order of two pieces of it), the metadata, the outline, and whether the document is accessible: tagged, with a language and a title, and conforming to PDF/UA or PDF/A. It reads a document from a file, from an object of an s3 resource, or from the last response of an http resource.

s3 on its own can say an object exists, its content type and its size. The text of a PDF sits in compressed content streams, so content should contain never matches it; this resource reads the document instead.

version: 2

containers:
  minio:
    image: cgr.dev/chainguard/minio:latest
    command: ["server", "/data"]
    ports:
      - "9000/tcp"
  verapdf:
    preset: verapdf        # only needed for the conformance step

app:
  command: go run ./cmd/server
  port: 8080

resources:
  agreements-storage:
    type: s3
    container: minio
    options:
      buckets:
        - cas
  app-client:
    type: http-client
    base_url: http://localhost:8080
  agreement-pdf:
    type: pdf
    options:
      validator: verapdf   # optional: the container that checks PDF/UA and PDF/A

Scenario: A deselected clause keeps its number in the country PDF
  When "app-client" sends "POST" to "/versions/AT/pdf"
  Then "agreements-storage" object "cas/CA_Version_No._07.07_AT-de.pdf" should exist within "30s"
  When "agreement-pdf" reads "agreements-storage" object "cas/CA_Version_No._07.07_AT-de.pdf"
  Then "agreement-pdf" text contains "9 Kryptowerte"
  And "agreement-pdf" text contains "Absichtlich frei gelassen"
  And "agreement-pdf" text contains "Version 07.07"
  And "agreement-pdf" text does not contain "{{"

Scenario: A bilingual version is sequential, not columns
  When "agreement-pdf" reads "agreements-storage" object "cas/CA_Version_No._07.07_LU-fr-en.pdf"
  Then "agreement-pdf" text "Conditions générales" appears before "General Terms and Conditions"

Scenario: The generated PDF is accessible
  When "app-client" sends "GET" to "/versions/AT/pdf"
  And "agreement-pdf" reads "app-client" response body
  Then "agreement-pdf" is tagged
  And "agreement-pdf" language is "de-AT"
  And "agreement-pdf" metadata "Title" is "Kundenvereinbarung"
  And "agreement-pdf" conforms to "PDF/UA-1"

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Meaning validator none The name of a container running veraPDF, normally one with preset: verapdf. Only conforms to needs it; without it that step fails and says so, and every other step works. timeout 2m How long one conformance check may take. veraPDF needs a few seconds for a long document, more under emulation.

docs.title: Reading a document
docs.text:
Three steps load a document; every other step asserts on the last one loaded.

Step Reads "agreement-pdf" reads file "out/ca.pdf" A file, relative to the directory tomato runs in, as shell and the s3 upload steps resolve paths. "agreement-pdf" reads "agreements-storage" object "cas/x.pdf" An object of the s3 resource named agreements-storage, as bucket/key, the same form that resource's own steps take. "agreement-pdf" reads "app-client" response body The body of the last response the http resource named app-client received. Send the request first.

The resource named in a step has to be of the right type: naming a redis resource in reads "app-cache" object fails with what it is. A document that does not parse fails the reading step with pdfcpu's reason, and the previous document stays loaded.

Before every scenario, reset drops the loaded document. Nothing else is kept or cleared; the validator container stays up.

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
tomato reads the text out of the content streams itself. It follows the document the way a viewer draws it, font by font, and rebuilds words and lines from where the glyphs land rather than from how the generator split the runs: Word writes a line as one run per kerning pair, fpdf and TCPDF one run per cell, and both read back as lines of words. The text of each page is lines separated by newlines; the document's text is its pages in order.

Matching is exact and case-sensitive, but whitespace is not significant: a phrase that breaks across a line, or that the generator spaced differently, matches what a person reads. text contains "9 Kryptowerte" finds it on any page; page "3" contains looks at one page, counted from 1; text "Conditions générales" appears before "General Terms and Conditions" fails when either is missing, and names the page the second one is on when the order is wrong. A failed assertion shows how many pages and characters were read and the start of the text.

What it does not do:

  • Reading order across columns. Text comes in the order the document draws it, which is reading order for generated documents and may interleave columns in a magazine layout.
  • Hyphenation. A word broken at a line end stays broken: cor- and ners on two lines.
  • Ligatures. ﬁ reads as ﬁ or as fi, whichever the font's ToUnicode map says. Assert on text around them when a document's font keeps them.
  • Glyphs with no text behind them. A font without a ToUnicode map (icon fonts, some subsetted CID fonts) reads as � per glyph.
  • Annotations, form fields and images. Text in a form field's appearance, a stamp or a scanned image is not read; there is no OCR.
  • Vertical writing. Rotated text is read along its baseline; vertical writing mode is not.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
metadata "Title" is "Kundenvereinbarung" reads the Info dictionary (Title, Author, Subject, Keywords, Creator, Producer, CreationDate, ModDate), and where the Info dictionary lacks an entry, the XMP metadata: dc:title, dc:creator, dc:description, pdf:Keywords, xmp:CreatorTool, pdf:Producer. PDF 2.0 and PDF/UA documents carry their title there. Keys are matched regardless of case.

language is "de-AT" reads the catalog's Lang entry, a BCP 47 tag, regardless of case. outline contains "7 Zinsen" matches the title of an entry of the document outline (the bookmarks a viewer shows as a table of contents) at any depth, exactly, after trimming whitespace; a failure lists the entries there are.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
is tagged passes when the catalog's MarkInfo says Marked and a structure tree (StructTreeRoot) is present. That is necessary for an accessible document, not sufficient: conforms to "PDF/UA-1" has veraPDF check every rule of the standard, and fails with the rules the document breaks:

the document from "app-client" response body does not conform to PDF/UA-1: 3 rules failed (PDF/UA-1 validation profile)
  7.1-3 (22 checks): Content shall be marked as Artifact or tagged as real content
      at root/document/pages[0]/contentStream[0]/content[0]/contentItem[0]
  7.21.4.1-1 (2 checks): The font programs for all fonts used for rendering within a conforming file shall be embedded within that file
      at root/document/pages[0]/contentStream[0]/operators[10]/font[0] Helvetica-Bold
  7.1-10 (1 check): The document catalog dictionary shall include a ViewerPreferences dictionary containing a DisplayDocTitle key, whose value shall be true
      at root

The levels it checks, and veraPDF's own id for each, which the step also accepts:

Level Id Standard PDF/UA-1, PDF/UA-2 ua1, ua2 ISO 14289, accessibility PDF/A-1a, PDF/A-1b 1a, 1b ISO 19005-1 PDF/A-2a, PDF/A-2b, PDF/A-2u 2a, 2b, 2u ISO 19005-2 PDF/A-3a, PDF/A-3b, PDF/A-3u 3a, 3b, 3u ISO 19005-3 PDF/A-4, PDF/A-4e, PDF/A-4f 4, 4e, 4f ISO 19005-4 WTPDF-1.0-Reuse, WTPDF-1.0-Accessibility wt1r, wt1a Well-Tagged PDF

docs.title: The verapdf preset
docs.text:
containers:
  verapdf:
    preset: verapdf

The preset runs verapdf/rest (a pinned version), the veraPDF consortium's REST service, and waits until /api/info answers on port 8080. The conformance step posts the loaded document to it and reads the report back, so nothing is written to disk and a remote Docker host works as well as a local one.

The image is published for amd64 only. On an arm64 machine Docker runs it under emulation: it works, and the JVM takes longer to start, which the preset's three-minute wait allows for. To run another build, set image:; anything serving the same REST API on port 8080 fits. env on the entry reaches the JVM: JAVA_OPTS: "-Xmx512m" for a larger heap.

docs.title: Between scenarios
docs.text: Reset drops the loaded document. The validator container stays up, and a scenario that asserts on a document reads it first.

docs.title: RabbitMQ configuration
docs.text: This guide covers how to configure RabbitMQ for integration testing with tomato.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: RabbitMQ is a popular message broker that implements AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol). Unlike Kafka's topic-based model, RabbitMQ uses an exchange/queue/binding model for message routing.

docs.title: RabbitMQ concepts
docs.text: Concept Description Queue A buffer that stores messages Exchange Routes messages to queues based on routing rules Binding A link between an exchange and a queue with an optional routing key Routing Key A message attribute used by exchanges to route messages

docs.title: Exchange types
docs.text: Type Description direct Routes messages to queues with matching routing key fanout Broadcasts messages to all bound queues (ignores routing key) topic Routes messages based on routing key patterns (wildcards: * single word, # zero or more words) headers Routes based on message headers instead of routing key

docs.title: Container setup
docs.text:
Add a RabbitMQ container to your tomato.yml:

containers:
  rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:3-alpine
    ports:
      - "5672/tcp"
    env:
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER: guest
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS: guest
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "5672"
      timeout: 30s

docs.title: Management UI (optional)
docs.text:
For debugging, you can use the management image which includes a web UI:

containers:
  rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:3-management-alpine
    ports:
      - "5672/tcp"
      - "15672/tcp"  # Management UI
    env:
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER: guest
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS: guest
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "5672"
      timeout: 30s

Access the management UI at http://localhost:<mapped-port> with credentials guest/guest.

docs.title: Resource configuration
docs.text:
Configure the RabbitMQ resource:

resources:
  orders-queue:
    type: rabbitmq
    container: rabbitmq
    options:
      user: guest
      password: guest
      vhost: /
      reset_strategy: purge

docs.title: Resource options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description user string guest RabbitMQ username password string guest RabbitMQ password vhost string / Virtual host to connect to reset_strategy string purge How to reset between scenarios queues list - Pre-declare queues on init exchanges list - Pre-declare exchanges on init bindings list - Pre-declare bindings on init

docs.title: Reset strategies
docs.text: Strategy Description purge Purge messages from all declared queues (recommended, fastest) delete_recreate Delete and recreate all declared queues and exchanges none No reset between scenarios

docs.title: Pre-declaring resources
docs.text:
You can pre-declare queues, exchanges, and bindings in the config:

resources:
  orders-queue:
    type: rabbitmq
    container: rabbitmq
    options:
      user: guest
      password: guest
      reset_strategy: purge
      queues:
        - name: orders
          durable: true
        - name: notifications
          auto_delete: true
      exchanges:
        - name: events
          type: topic
          durable: true
        - name: broadcast
          type: fanout
      bindings:
        - queue: orders
          exchange: events
          routing_key: "order.*"
        - queue: notifications
          exchange: broadcast

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
Here's a complete tomato.yml with RabbitMQ:

version: 2

settings:
  timeout: 5m
  fail_fast: false
  output: pretty

containers:
  rabbitmq:
    image: rabbitmq:3-alpine
    ports:
      - "5672/tcp"
    env:
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER: guest
      RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS: guest
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "5672"
      timeout: 30s

resources:
  orders-queue:
    type: rabbitmq
    container: rabbitmq
    options:
      user: guest
      password: guest
      reset_strategy: purge

features:
  paths:
    - ./features

docs.title: Basic queue operations
docs.text:
Feature: Order Processing

  Scenario: Orders are queued for processing
    Given "orders-queue" declares queue "orders"
    And "orders-queue" consumes from queue "orders"
    When "orders-queue" publishes json to queue "orders":
      """
      {"order_id": "123", "amount": 99.99}
      """
    Then "orders-queue" receives from queue "orders" within "5s"
    And "orders-queue" last message contains:
      """
      order_id
      """

docs.title: Topic exchange routing
docs.text:
Scenario: Route orders by type
  Given "orders-queue" declares exchange "orders" of type "topic"
  And "orders-queue" declares queue "domestic-orders"
  And "orders-queue" declares queue "international-orders"
  And "orders-queue" binds queue "domestic-orders" to exchange "orders" with routing key "order.domestic.*"
  And "orders-queue" binds queue "international-orders" to exchange "orders" with routing key "order.international.*"
  And "orders-queue" consumes from queue "domestic-orders"
  When "orders-queue" publishes to exchange "orders" with routing key "order.domestic.new":
    """
    New domestic order
    """
  Then "orders-queue" receives from queue "domestic-orders" within "5s":
    """
    New domestic order
    """

docs.title: Fanout exchange broadcasting
docs.text:
Scenario: Broadcast notifications to all subscribers
  Given "orders-queue" declares exchange "notifications" of type "fanout"
  And "orders-queue" declares queue "email-service"
  And "orders-queue" declares queue "push-service"
  And "orders-queue" declares queue "sms-service"
  And "orders-queue" binds queue "email-service" to exchange "notifications"
  And "orders-queue" binds queue "push-service" to exchange "notifications"
  And "orders-queue" binds queue "sms-service" to exchange "notifications"
  And "orders-queue" consumes from queue "email-service"
  And "orders-queue" consumes from queue "push-service"
  When "orders-queue" publishes to exchange "notifications" with routing key "":
    """
    System maintenance in 1 hour
    """
  Then "orders-queue" receives from queue "email-service" within "5s":
    """
    System maintenance in 1 hour
    """
  And "orders-queue" receives from queue "push-service" within "5s":
    """
    System maintenance in 1 hour
    """

See RabbitMQ Steps for the complete list of available steps.

docs.title: Connection refused
docs.text:
If tests fail with "connection refused":

  1. Verify RabbitMQ container is healthy: docker ps
  2. Check the mapped port: docker port <container_id>
  3. Ensure credentials match configuration

docs.title: Consumer not receiving messages
docs.text:
1. Ensure consumes from queue is called before publishing
  2. Verify the queue exists and is bound to the correct exchange
  3. Check routing keys match the binding patterns

docs.title: Messages not routing
docs.text: For topic exchanges, verify your routing key patterns: - * matches exactly one word (e.g., order.* matches order.created but not order.created.urgent) - # matches zero or more words (e.g., order.# matches order, order.created, and order.created.urgent)

docs.title: Queue already exists with different properties
docs.text: If you get "PRECONDITION_FAILED" errors: - Queues and exchanges are idempotent but properties must match - Either delete the queue manually or use reset_strategy: delete_recreate

docs.title: Redis configuration
docs.text: This guide covers how to configure Redis for integration testing with tomato.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Redis is an in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, and message broker. Tomato's Redis handler supports strings, hashes, lists, and sets.

docs.title: Preset
docs.text:
The shortest setup is the redis preset:

containers:
  redis:
    preset: redis

resources:
  sessions-cache:
    type: redis
    container: redis

docs.title: Cluster mode and TLS, as ElastiCache runs it
docs.text:
A service that talks to ElastiCache with cluster mode and in-transit encryption usually has one Redis client, and it is a cluster client over TLS:

redis.NewClusterClient(&redis.ClusterOptions{
    Addrs:     []string{cfg.URL},
    TLSConfig: &tls.Config{}, // verifies against the system roots
})

A plain Redis container can't stand in for that server. cluster and tls make the preset one that can, without a change to the service:

containers:
  redis:
    preset: redis
    cluster: true   # one node owning all 16384 slots
    tls: true       # TLS only, with a certificate from a CA made for the run

app:
  command: ./bin/app
  env:
    REDIS_URL: "{{.redis.host}}:{{.redis.port.6379}}"
    SSL_CERT_FILE: "{{.redis.ca_file}}"   # trust the run's CA
    # On macOS, when go.mod says a go version below 1.27 (see below):
    # GODEBUG: x509sslcertoverrideplatform=1

resources:
  sessions-cache:
    type: redis
    container: redis   # connects the same way: cluster, TLS, the run's CA

The redis steps work as they do against a single server:

Then "sessions-cache" key "claim:{{id}}" exists

What each option does:

Option What tomato does cluster: true Starts the server with cluster mode on and gives the node every slot. The node announces 127.0.0.1 and the host port tomato picked before it started, so a cluster client on the host follows CLUSTER SLOTS to an address it can dial. To choose that port, list it in ports ("16379:6379"); tomato announces it instead. tls: true Makes a CA and a server certificate for localhost and 127.0.0.1 for the run, and serves TLS only: a plain client is refused, as ElastiCache refuses it. {{.redis.ca_file}} is the CA's path on your machine; tomato removes it when the run ends.

Both set the redis resource's cluster and tls_ca_file options, so it reaches the server the way the app does. Resets flush every key, as they do on a single server.

Things to know:

  • The app runs as a command (app.command). The node announces an address on your machine, and the CA is a file there; neither reaches an app in a container.
  • SSL_CERT_FILE on macOS depends on the service's Go version. On Linux, Go and the clients built on OpenSSL (Python, Ruby) trust the file it names; Node needs NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS instead, and Java a trust store. On macOS (and Windows), Go honours it since Go 1.27, but only when the main module says go 1.27 or later; an older go line keeps verifying through the system. For those, add GODEBUG: x509sslcertoverrideplatform=1 to app.env. Either way the service has to be built with Go 1.27 or later: earlier releases ignore SSL_CERT_FILE on macOS, whatever is set.
  • A network resource can't stand in front of a cluster. The client follows the address the node announces, which takes it around the proxy.
  • settings.containers.reuse can't be used with them. A reused container keeps the CA and the port of the run that started it.

docs.title: Container setup
docs.text:
Without the preset, add a Redis container to your tomato.yml:

containers:
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports:
      - "6379/tcp"
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "6379"
      timeout: 30s

docs.title: With password authentication
docs.text:
containers:
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: redis-server --requirepass mysecretpassword
    ports:
      - "6379/tcp"
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "6379"
      timeout: 30s

docs.title: With persistence (optional)
docs.text:
For tests that need data persistence across container restarts:

containers:
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: redis-server --appendonly yes
    ports:
      - "6379/tcp"
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "6379"
      timeout: 30s

docs.title: Resource configuration
docs.text:
Configure the Redis resource:

resources:
  app-cache:
    type: redis
    container: redis
    options:
      db: 0
      password: ""
      reset_strategy: flush

docs.title: Resource options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description db int 0 Redis database number (0-15) password string "" Redis password (if authentication enabled) reset_strategy string flush How to reset between scenarios reset_pattern string * Pattern for selective key deletion (when using pattern strategy) cluster bool false Connect as a cluster client (the preset's cluster: true sets it) tls_ca_file string Connect over TLS, trusting this CA (the preset's tls: true sets it)

docs.title: Reset strategies
docs.text: Strategy Description flush Flush all keys in the database (recommended, fastest) pattern Delete keys matching reset_pattern (useful for shared databases)

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
Here's a complete tomato.yml with Redis:

version: 2

settings:
  timeout: 5m
  fail_fast: false
  output: pretty

containers:
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports:
      - "6379/tcp"
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "6379"
      timeout: 30s

resources:
  app-cache:
    type: redis
    container: redis
    options:
      db: 0
      reset_strategy: flush

features:
  paths:
    - ./features

docs.title: String operations
docs.text:
Feature: Caching

  Scenario: Cache user data
    Given "app-cache" key "user:123" is "John Doe"
    Then "app-cache" key "user:123" exists
    And "app-cache" key "user:123" has value "John Doe"

  Scenario: Cache with expiration
    Given "app-cache" key "session:abc" is "token123" with TTL "1h"
    Then "app-cache" key "session:abc" has TTL greater than "3500" seconds

  Scenario: Store JSON data
    Given "app-cache" key "config" is:
      """
      {"debug": true, "timeout": 30}
      """
    Then "app-cache" key "config" contains "debug"

docs.title: Hash operations
docs.text:
Scenario: Store user profile as hash
  Given "app-cache" hash "user:100" has fields:
    | field | value           |
    | name  | Alice           |
    | email | alice@test.com  |
    | role  | admin           |
  Then "app-cache" hash "user:100" field "name" is "Alice"
  And "app-cache" hash "user:100" contains:
    | field | value          |
    | email | alice@test.com |

docs.title: List operations
docs.text:
Scenario: Manage task queue
  Given "app-cache" list "tasks" has values:
    | process-order-1 |
    | process-order-2 |
    | send-email-3    |
  Then "app-cache" list "tasks" has "3" items
  And "app-cache" list "tasks" contains "process-order-1"

docs.title: Set operations
docs.text:
Scenario: Track unique visitors
  Given "app-cache" set "visitors" has members:
    | user-1 |
    | user-2 |
    | user-3 |
  Then "app-cache" set "visitors" has "3" members
  And "app-cache" set "visitors" contains "user-2"

docs.title: Counter operations
docs.text:
Scenario: Track page views
  Given "app-cache" key "pageviews" is "100"
  When "app-cache" key "pageviews" is incremented
  Then "app-cache" key "pageviews" has value "101"
  When "app-cache" key "pageviews" is incremented by "10"
  Then "app-cache" key "pageviews" has value "111"

See Redis Steps for the complete list of available steps.

docs.title: Multiple Redis databases
docs.text:
You can configure multiple Redis resources pointing to different databases:

resources:
  app-cache:
    type: redis
    container: redis
    options:
      db: 0
      reset_strategy: flush

  sessions-cache:
    type: redis
    container: redis
    options:
      db: 1
      reset_strategy: flush

docs.title: Connection refused
docs.text:
If tests fail with "connection refused":

  1. Verify Redis container is running: docker ps
  2. Check port mapping: docker port <container_id>
  3. Ensure no firewall is blocking the connection

docs.title: Authentication failed
docs.text:
If using password authentication:

  1. Verify password matches in container command and resource options
  2. Check for special characters that may need escaping

docs.title: Keys not being reset
docs.text:
If keys persist between scenarios:

  1. Verify reset_strategy is set (defaults to flush)
  2. If using pattern strategy, verify reset_pattern matches your keys

docs.title: S3 configuration
docs.text: This guide covers how to configure S3-compatible object storage for integration testing with tomato.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The s3 resource talks to any S3-compatible endpoint. In tests that usually means MinIO or LocalStack, but the same resource works against a real bucket if you point it at one.

Because it speaks the S3 protocol rather than a vendor API, one set of steps covers all three.

docs.title: MinIO
docs.text:
MinIO needs an explicit server command — the image's default entrypoint only prints help.

containers:
  minio:
    image: cgr.dev/chainguard/minio:latest
    command: ["server", "/data"]
    ports:
      - "9000/tcp"
    env:
      MINIO_ROOT_USER: minioadmin
      MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: minioadmin
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "9000"
      timeout: 30s

docs.title: LocalStack
docs.text:
containers:
  localstack:
    image: localstack/localstack:3
    ports:
      - "4566/tcp"
    env:
      SERVICES: s3
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "4566"
      timeout: 90s

docs.title: Resource configuration
docs.text:
resources:
  orders-storage:
    type: s3
    container: minio
    options:
      buckets:
        - uploads
        - reports

minio is accepted as an alias for type: s3.

The endpoint is derived from the container automatically. Tomato probes port 9000 (MinIO) and then 4566 (LocalStack), so neither image needs a port option.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default Description endpoint (from container) Explicit endpoint, e.g. localhost:9000. Scheme is optional. port 9000 then 4566 Container port to resolve the endpoint from. region us-east-1 AWS region. access_key minioadmin Access key ID. secret_key minioadmin Secret access key. use_ssl false Use https:// when building the endpoint. force_path_style true Path-style addressing. Required by MinIO and LocalStack. buckets (none) Buckets created at startup, before any scenario runs. reset_strategy purge purge or delete. See below. reset_buckets (all buckets) Limit reset to these buckets. reset_exclude (none) Buckets reset never touches.

docs.title: Connecting without a container
docs.text:
Point the resource at an endpoint directly to test against something tomato does not manage:

resources:
  orders-storage:
    type: s3
    options:
      endpoint: "https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com"
      region: eu-central-1
      use_ssl: true
      force_path_style: false
      access_key: "${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"
      secret_key: "${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}"

Reset deletes objects

Reset is destructive by design. Against a real account, set scope it with reset_buckets.

docs.title: Reset behaviour
docs.text:
Following tomato's clean-state principle, every scenario starts with empty storage.

Strategy Behaviour purge (default) Deletes every object, keeps the buckets. delete Deletes the buckets entirely, then recreates those listed in buckets. none Leaves storage untouched.

By default reset covers every bucket on the endpoint, not just the ones in buckets. That way buckets your application creates at runtime are cleaned up too. Narrow it with reset_buckets, or protect individual buckets with reset_exclude:

resources:
  orders-storage:
    type: s3
    container: minio
    options:
      buckets: [uploads]
      reset_exclude: [fixtures]   # seeded once in a before_all hook

A resource cannot opt out of reset altogether: every resource is wiped before every scenario. reset_exclude is how a bucket survives, and a before_all hook is where its contents are seeded.

docs.title: Wiring your application
docs.text:
Pass the endpoint to the application under test with container templates:

app:
  command: go run ./cmd/server
  port: 8080
  env:
    S3_ENDPOINT: "http://{{.minio.host}}:{{.minio.port.9000}}"
    S3_ACCESS_KEY: minioadmin
    S3_SECRET_KEY: minioadmin
    S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE: "true"

docs.title: Object paths
docs.text:
Every object step takes a single bucket/key path. An s3:// prefix is stripped if present.

Given "orders-storage" object "uploads/2026/01/report.pdf" is "..."

Writing to a bucket that does not exist creates it, so seeding steps do not need a bucket ... exists line first.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Feature: Report export

  Scenario: Exporting writes a report to S3
    Given "orders-db" table "orders" has values:
      | id | total |
      | 1  | 42.00 |
    When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/exports"
    Then "orders-client" response status is "202"
    And "orders-storage" object "reports/orders.csv" should exist within "10s"
    And "orders-storage" object "reports/orders.csv" content should contain "42.00"

The within steps matter here: applications usually upload in the background, so a plain should exist would race the write.

docs.title: ScyllaDB configuration
docs.text: This guide covers how to configure ScyllaDB or Apache Cassandra for integration testing with tomato.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The scylladb resource talks CQL, so it works with both ScyllaDB and Apache Cassandra (type: cassandra is an alias). Tomato creates the keyspace, runs your schema files, truncates tables between scenarios, and provides steps to seed and assert on data. See the ScyllaDB step reference for all steps.

docs.title: ScyllaDB
docs.text:
containers:
  scylla:
    image: scylladb/scylla:6.2
    # Single shard and little memory: enough for tests and CI runners
    command: ["--smp", "1", "--memory", "512M", "--overprovisioned", "1", "--developer-mode", "1"]
    ports:
      - "9042/tcp"
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "9042"
      timeout: 120s

docs.title: Apache Cassandra
docs.text:
containers:
  cassandra:
    image: cassandra:5
    env:
      MAX_HEAP_SIZE: 512M
      HEAP_NEWSIZE: 128M
    ports:
      - "9042/tcp"
    wait_for:
      type: port
      target: "9042"
      timeout: 180s

The port opens before the node serves CQL. The resource keeps retrying until a query succeeds (ready_timeout, 90s by default), so the port wait is enough.

docs.title: Resource configuration
docs.text:
resources:
  app-db:
    type: scylladb
    container: scylla
    options:
      keyspace: app
      schema:
        - ./fixtures/schema.cql
        - ./fixtures/reference-data.cql
      exclude:
        - countries

docs.title: Resource options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description keyspace string - Keyspace for unqualified table names. Also accepted as the resource's database field create_keyspace bool true Create keyspace if it doesn't exist, with SimpleStrategy replication_factor int 1 Replication factor used when creating the keyspace schema string or list - CQL files run once at startup, after the keyspace is created keyspaces list [keyspace] Keyspaces whose tables are truncated on reset tables list - If set, only these tables are truncated on reset exclude list - Tables never truncated; table or keyspace.table consistency string ONE Consistency level, e.g. ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM user / password string - Credentials for PasswordAuthenticator hosts list - Connect to host:port instead of a container ready_timeout duration 90s How long to wait for CQL to accept queries

docs.title: Schema files
docs.text:
Schema files are plain CQL scripts. Statements are split on ;, and semicolons inside strings, quoted identifiers, $$ strings and comments are ignored.

-- fixtures/schema.cql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS app.users (
    id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    email text,
    created_at timestamp,
    tags set<text>
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS app.countries (
    code text PRIMARY KEY,
    name text
);

INSERT INTO app.countries (code, name) VALUES ('DE', 'Germany');

If your application creates its own schema on startup (for example with a migration tool), you can leave schema out and let the app do it.

docs.title: Seeding data
docs.text:
table ... has values: inserts rows with INSERT ... JSON, so cells are written as text and CQL converts them to the column type (int, uuid, timestamp, boolean, ...). A cell holding a JSON array or object fills a list, set, map or UDT column, and null writes a null.

Given "app-db" table "users" has values:
  | id                                   | email          | created_at           | tags          |
  | 11111111-1111-4111-a111-111111111111 | alice@test.com | 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z | ["admin"]     |

docs.title: Assertions
docs.text:
CQL has no global row order, so table ... contains: and query result of ... contains: match rows in any order. query ... returns: compares rows in the order the query returns them. Use it with a WHERE on the partition key when order matters.

Values are compared as text: timestamps in RFC 3339 UTC (2026-01-01T00:00:00Z), UUIDs in canonical form, collections as JSON. An unset text or number column reads back as its zero value ("", 0), as gocql reports it.

docs.title: Wiring the app
docs.text:
Pass the container address to your app like any other dependency:

app:
  command: java -jar build/libs/app.jar
  env:
    SPRING_CASSANDRA_CONTACT_POINTS: "{{.scylla.host}}:{{.scylla.port.9042}}"
    SPRING_CASSANDRA_KEYSPACE_NAME: app
    SPRING_CASSANDRA_LOCAL_DATACENTER: datacenter1

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
CQL resources work with sql and sql_file hooks:

hooks:
  before_all:
    - sql_file: ./fixtures/extra.cql
      resource: app-db

docs.title: Adding a step or a resource
docs.text:
This page is for people changing tomato itself. For writing a suite with tomato, start at Getting started.

Two rules shape everything below. Steps, config fields, CLI flags and Action inputs are a stable surface: never rename or remove one in place. And step wording is the product — users read it from tomato steps, and tomato docs generates the reference from the same definitions, so the wording you write is the documentation.

docs.title: Adding a step to a resource
docs.text:
1. Add a StepDef to the resource's Steps() in internal/resource/<name>/, with Group, Pattern (use {resource} where the resource name goes), Description, Example and Handler.

  2. Use it in a scenario in tests/features/<resource>.feature. CI fails when any step of any resource type is unused — check locally with:

    ./bin/tomato coverage -c tests/tomato.yml --all-types

  3. Regenerate the reference and commit the result:

    go build -o tomato . && ./tomato docs

The Example is not decoration. It appears in the generated page, and TestDocsExamplesUseRealSteps checks every Gherkin snippet in docs/ against the live patterns, so an example that does not parse as a real step fails CI.

docs.title: Adding a resource type
docs.text:
1. The handler. Create internal/resource/<name>/<name>.go with

    func New(name string, cfg config.Resource, cm *container.Manager) (*Name, error)

    implementing resource.Handler: Name, Init, Ready, Reset, RegisterSteps, Cleanup. The package imports internal/resource and nothing from another resource — TestResourcesDoNotImportEachOther enforces that. If two resources need the same helper, it belongs in internal/resource or internal/jsonmatch.

  2. Reset. Reset runs before every scenario and has to leave the resource genuinely clean, including state that survives the obvious command — Postgres truncates with RESTART IDENTITY because plain TRUNCATE leaves sequences advanced, which made scenarios order-dependent. Exclude only what the application needs to exist, such as migration tables.

  3. Steps. Implement Steps() resource.StepCategory and call resource.RegisterStepsToGodog(ctx, r.name, r.Steps()) from RegisterSteps.

  4. Register it once, in internal/registry/registry.go: add it to handlerFactories and to canonicalTypes. The first makes it buildable by tomato run and accepted by tomato validate; the second gives it a documentation page and a place in tomato steps. Two tests pin the lists against each other, so missing one fails CI. Add it to ContainerBasedTypes() if it normally points at a container.

  5. Documentation. Add a page under docs/configuration/ for its options, and add it and the generated docs/resources/ page to the nav in mkdocs.yml. The step reference generates itself.

  6. Tests. Unit tests in the resource's own package, a container in tests/tomato.yml, and tests/features/<name>.feature exercising every step.

  7. Changelog. A line under ## [Unreleased].

Agree the config shape and the step wording in an issue before writing the code. Both are a stable surface from the moment they ship.

docs.title: Changing or removing a step or an option
docs.text:
Add the replacement, then mark the old one:

{
    Pattern:    `^"{resource}" old wording$`,
    Deprecated: "use the new wording instead",
    Handler:    r.handler,
}

A deprecated step keeps working and warns once per run, and the generated reference labels it. Note the replacement under Deprecated in the changelog. See Stability for how long it has to stay.

docs.title: Before opening the pull request
docs.text:
• make coverage passes. It is what CI runs: unit and integration coverage merged, every resource step used by a scenario, and the floors in .coverage-min. When coverage rises, raise the floors in the same PR.
  • ./tomato docs has been run and the result committed.
  • If the change touches timing or the infrastructure the suite runs on — a broker, a database image, startup order, a reset, anything concurrent — run the affected features several times. One green run proves very little about a race.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page provides an overview of tomato's internal architecture and how components interact during test execution.

docs.title: High-level overview
docs.text:
tomato is designed around three core concepts:

  1. Containers - Docker containers managed via Testcontainers
  2. Resources - Abstractions over external services (databases, APIs, message queues)
  3. Handlers - Step definitions that interact with resources

docs.title: What is in the repository
docs.text:
tomato is a Go program with a web UI, a documentation site, and two things it ships besides the binary. The root reads more clearly once you know which is which, and which of them CI actually checks.

Path What it is Checked by CI main.go, command/, internal/ The Go program. main.go is the entry point, command/ is one file per CLI command, internal/ is everything else make test, make coverage ui/ The web UI tomato ui serves: a React app built by Vite with pnpm. pnpm build writes the bundle into command/ui_assets/dist, which the binary embeds, so the bundle is committed too make ui-test runs its unit tests; make ui-check fails on a stale bundle tests/ tomato's integration suite: tomato testing itself against real containers. tests/tomato.yml plus tests/features/*.feature make coverage; every step of every resource must be used by a scenario docs/ The documentation site, built with mkdocs.yml. docs/resources/ and docs/index.md are generated — the docs workflow overwrites them with tomato docs and README.md before deploying, so edit the generator or the README, never those files regenerated and deployed, not checked for drift action.yml, install.sh The two shipped deliverables besides the binary: the GitHub Action and the install script no — neither is exercised by a workflow scripts/ report-coverage.sh, which builds the PR coverage comment and enforces the gates in .coverage-min runs in make coverage .tomato/, bin/, coverage/ Generated at runtime, all git-ignored —

docs.title: Where the code lives
docs.text: Package Responsibility command/ One file per CLI command, plus the step-docs generator internal/config tomato.yml parsing, defaults, validation, preset expansion internal/container Container lifecycle via Testcontainers, wait strategies, logs internal/apprunner Starting the application under test, app.env templating internal/resource The contract every resource implements: Handler, step definitions, the variable store internal/resource/<name> One package per resource type, with its step definitions and nothing else's internal/registry Builds resources from config and is the only package that knows the full set internal/grpcschema Naming and resolving gRPC methods against file descriptors, and status code names, shared by the grpc client and grpc-server internal/jsonmatch Dotted-path lookup and tomato's @ matchers, shared by every resource that asserts on JSON internal/runner godog wiring, hooks, tag filtering, reset between scenarios internal/formatter Console, JUnit and Cucumber report output internal/presets Files copied into preset containers (the MSK IAM jar) internal/pdffixture The PDF documents the pdf resource's tests assert on, generated deterministically: the test app serves them and tests/testdata/pdf holds committed copies internal/grpcfixture The gRPC service the grpc-server resource's tests stub, as a descriptor: the test app calls it and tests/testdata/grpc holds the committed descriptor set and a .proto rendering internal/runlog Per-run log directory under .tomato/runs/

docs.title: Why one package per resource
docs.text:
Each resource package imports internal/resource and nothing from any other resource, so a change to the Kafka steps cannot break the Postgres ones, and a contributor adding steps to one resource reads one directory. go build ./internal/resource/postgres/ compiles that resource alone.

A resource type is registered in exactly one place, handlerFactories in internal/registry/registry.go. That table and canonicalTypes beside it are the only lists of resources in the codebase: the commands ask the registry rather than naming resources themselves.

docs.title: Design: network faults
docs.text:
Status: proposal, with a proof of concept on feat/network-faults.

A network resource puts a proxy between the application under test and one of its dependency containers, so a scenario can make that dependency slow, cut its connections, make it hang or refuse connections, and then check what the application does. It works the same way for every dependency tomato runs in a container, because it works on TCP: Postgres, MySQL-compatible databases, Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ, ScyllaDB, MinIO and anything else.

This page has three parts: what a spike found, the interface users write, and what the reports show.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: Production fails in ways a healthy test environment never does: a database that answers in 800 ms, a broker that drops every connection during a failover, a cache that accepts a connection and never answers. tomato can already stop and pause containers (lifecycle) and make its own HTTP and gRPC stubs slow or unreachable. What it cannot do is degrade a real dependency without taking it down, and only for the application: the faults must not reach the steps that check the result.

docs.title: Spike
docs.text:
The spike embedded Toxiproxy v2.13.0 in a Go process, in front of real containers, and drove each one with the client library tomato already uses, configured the way an application would be. Each fault was applied to a pooled connection, then removed, and the client's recovery timed.

Fault Postgres (lib/pq) Redis (go-redis) S3 (MinIO, aws-sdk-go-v2) RabbitMQ (amqp091) Kafka (sarama) latency 300 ms 302 ms 302 ms 312 ms 302 ms 304 ms hang (timeout 0) client ignored its deadline, stayed blocked i/o timeout at 2 s deadline exceeded deadline exceeded deadline exceeded reset (reset_peer) connection reset by peer EOF request failed EOF EOF refuse (proxy disabled) connection refused connection refused connection refused connection refused connection refused fail the next 2 connections 2 fail, 3rd ok, pool untouched same same same same after the fault is removed recovers in 1 try 1 try 1 try never: no reconnect 1 try packet_loss 30 % 5 of 10 fail 3 of 10 4 of 10 (connection already dead) 7 of 10, "correlation ID didn't match"

Two of those cells are the point of the feature: they are bugs an application would ship. A service on lib/pq hangs for good when its database stops answering, unless it sets a TCP or statement timeout; a service on amqp091 never recovers from a dropped connection unless it reconnects itself.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
1. Embedding works. toxiproxy.NewServer, NewProxy, Proxy.Start and Stop, and Toxics.AddToxicJson / RemoveToxic are exported and enough to run proxies in tomato's process without Toxiproxy's HTTP API. Its logging goes to a zerolog.Nop().
  2. Go 1.27. Toxiproxy v2.13.0 requires Go 1.27; v2.12.0 builds with 1.23 but has no packet_loss. The proof of concept moves tomato to Go 1.27.
  3. Faults reach open connections. Adding a toxic splices it into every live connection, so a fault applied in the middle of a scenario affects the application's pooled connections at once, which is what a scenario wants.
  4. A disabled proxy keeps its port. Stop closes the listener and every open connection; Start listens on the same port again, so the application's configured address stays valid.
  5. Toxiproxy cannot count connections or fail only some of them reproducibly. toxicity is rolled with Go's global, unseeded random source, and rolled again for every live connection whenever another toxic is added. So tomato adds one toxic of its own, the gate, installed when a proxy starts and before any connection exists. Toxiproxy creates a stateful toxic's state once per connection, when it opens, so the gate decides there whether the connection fails ("the next 2", or a seeded percentage) and counts it. The spike confirmed it on all five protocols: exactly the next two new connections failed, the pooled ones were untouched, and the same seed gives the same pattern.
  6. ResetToxics removes the gate too. tomato removes its own faults by name instead.
  7. Unknown attributes are ignored silently. {"rate": 0.3} instead of {"loss_rate": 0.3} gives a toxic that does nothing. tomato builds every toxic from typed values, never from user JSON.
  8. packet_loss drops chunks of the TCP stream, not IP packets. TCP would retransmit a lost packet; this loses bytes the protocol expected, so the client sees a stall or a garbled stream. It is a useful fault, but not "packet loss", and the step says what it does.
  9. Kafka needs its listeners rearranged. A Kafka client dials the bootstrap address once, then the address the broker advertises. With a proxy only in front of the bootstrap port, every fault after the first request was bypassed (the "naive" run: latency 5 ms, hang and reset had no effect). With the broker advertising the proxy's port, every fault worked, and a second listener advertising its own port gave tomato's kafka resource a direct path while the application's link hung (produce in 8 ms). tomato already picks the broker's host ports before it starts, so the kafka preset can do both.
  10. Only the application goes through the proxy. The application learns a dependency's address from {{.postgres.port.5432}} in app.env, while tomato's own resources ask the container manager. Pointing the template at the proxy keeps every assertion step on the direct path.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
One network resource per dependency container:

containers:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    ports: ["5432/tcp"]

app:
  command: ./orders
  env:
    DATABASE_URL: "postgres://test:test@{{.postgres.host}}:{{.postgres.port.5432}}/test"

resources:
  orders-db:
    type: postgres
    container: postgres

  postgres-network:
    type: network
    container: postgres      # the dependency the application reaches through it
    options:
      ports: [5432]          # default: every port the container exposes
      seed: 42               # default: random, printed at the start of the run

Nothing else changes. {{.postgres.port.5432}} now resolves to the proxy's port, and orders-db still connects straight to the container. With the kafka preset, the broker advertises the proxy to the application and a direct listener to tomato's kafka resource.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Every fault lasts until the scenario ends or the network is healed. Each one also takes for "<duration>", after which it heals by itself, which is what retry and reconnect code has to survive.

Step On the wire Looks to the application like "postgres-network" adds latency "300ms" delays every response a slow dependency "postgres-network" adds latency "300ms" with jitter "100ms" random ±100 ms an uneven one "minio-network" limits bandwidth to "64KB/s" throttles responses a slow link "postgres-network" stops responding accepts, forwards nothing a hung dependency, a partition "redis-network" resets connections TCP RST on every connection a crash, a failover "kafka-network" refuses connections closes the listener and open connections the dependency is down "postgres-network" fails the next "2" connections the next two new connections close at once a dependency coming back up "postgres-network" fails "30%" of new connections seeded, per connection an intermittently failing one "kafka-network" loses "30%" of the data drops chunks of the stream a garbled or stalled link "rabbitmq-network" flaps every "2s" refuses, then accepts, in turn a dependency restarting in a loop "postgres-network" is healthy clears every fault

and two to check what the application did about it:

Step Checks "postgres-network" has seen "3" connections new connections since the scenario started, so a retry or a reconnect is something to assert "rabbitmq-network" sees a new connection within "10s" the application reconnected

Before every scenario the resource heals the network, resets its counts and stops its timers, before any other resource resets, so postgres truncates and kafka recreates topics over a healthy link.

Scenario: an order survives a database failover
  Given "postgres-network" resets connections for "3s"
  When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
    """
    {"id": "ord-1", "total": 1999}
    """
  Then "orders-client" response status is "201"
  And "postgres-network" has seen "2" connections

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Command mode only. In container mode (app.build) the application reaches postgres:5432 over the Docker network, past a proxy in tomato's process. A proxy container on that network is the follow-up.
  • TCP only, and blind to the protocol. It cannot fail only the INSERTs or only one Kafka topic. For HTTP and gRPC dependencies, the http-server and grpc-server stubs already answer late or refuse connections, per request.
  • Kafka through the preset. A hand-configured broker has to advertise the proxy itself.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
A fault nobody can see in the report makes a confusing failure, so each surface says which faults were on, when, and what they did.

At the start of the run, next to the containers:

  ✓ postgres
  ⇄ postgres-network  app → 127.0.0.1:51726 → postgres:5432  (seed 42)

On a failing step, in every format, the error says which faults were active and since which step, after the step's own error. The text is added by the wrapper every step handler already goes through (internal/resource/stepdef.go), and the error still unwraps to the step's own, so the diff tomato ui draws for a failed comparison is unchanged:

expected status 200, got 502
while the network was faulty:
  minio-network resets connections (step 3, 5s left)
  minio-network has seen 1 connection this scenario, 0 failed
  postgres-network adds latency 300ms (step 2)

In the tomato event stream, which tomato ui reads, every step_end carries the network events recorded while the step ran, with absolute timestamps, and the faults that were active. A network resource records its events the way the browser resource records screenshots (resource.RecordNetworkEvent, drained by the formatter at the step's end); events after the last step go on the scenario_end.

{"type": "step_end", "step": "\"minio-network\" resets connections for \"5s\"",
 "status": "passed",
 "network": {
   "events": [{"at": "2026-10-21T07:32:07.068+02:00", "resource": "minio-network",
               "kind": "applied", "detail": "resets connections for 5s"}],
   "active": ["minio-network resets connections (step 3, 5s left)",
              "postgres-network adds latency 300ms (step 2)"]}}

The kinds are applied, healed (by the step, or when its duration ran out), and connection (one the gate failed).

In tomato ui, a step that ran while a fault was on has a band and a badge naming the networks, with the faults on hover; the step during which something changed lists it with its time:

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
1. The proof of concept, on feat/network-faults: the network resource with every fault above, for and healing, the connection count and wait, the kafka preset's listeners, the events and the failing-step summary in every report, and the steps marked in tomato ui. tests/features/network.feature runs each fault against Postgres, Redis, MinIO, Kafka and RabbitMQ through the test app's own clients.
  2. Then: container mode, with a proxy container on tomato's network.
  3. Then, if suites ask for them: faults on the request direction only, and per-port faults for a container that exposes several.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
This guide takes you from nothing to a passing suite in seven steps.

Once it passes, read Writing a Suite — it covers the habits that make a suite worth trusting, in particular asserting the effects your application produces rather than only the response it returns.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker — tomato starts your test containers
  • Go 1.26+ — only for the go install and from-source methods

docs.title: Quick install (recommended)
docs.text: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tomatool/tomato/main/install.sh | sh

docs.title: Using Go
docs.text: go install github.com/tomatool/tomato@latest

docs.title: Using Homebrew
docs.text: brew install tomatool/tap/tomato

docs.title: Verify installation
docs.text: tomato --version

docs.title: 2. Create a project
docs.text:
Create a new project with the init command:

mkdir my-project && cd my-project
tomato init

This creates: - tomato.yml - Main configuration file - features/ - Directory for your feature files

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text:
my-project/
├── tomato.yml           # Main configuration
├── features/
│   └── example.feature  # Gherkin test files
└── fixtures/            # Optional: SQL scripts, test data

docs.title: 3. Describe your dependencies
docs.text:
tomato.yml says what your service needs and how the scenarios reach it. The examples on this page test an orders service that stores orders in Postgres and publishes them to Kafka:

version: 2

# Infrastructure tomato starts, named after the software
containers:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    env: { POSTGRES_USER: test, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test, POSTGRES_DB: orders }
    ports: ["5432/tcp"]
    wait_for: { type: exec, target: "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U test" }
  kafka:
    preset: kafka

# Your service
app:
  command: ./orders
  port: 8080
  ready: { type: http, path: /health }
  env:
    DATABASE_URL: "postgres://test:test@{{.postgres.host}}:{{.postgres.port.5432}}/orders"
    KAFKA_BROKERS: "{{.kafka.host}}:{{.kafka.port.9092}}"

# What the scenarios talk to, named <whose>-<role>
resources:
  orders-client:                # calls the orders service
    type: http
    base_url: http://localhost:8080
  orders-db:                    # the orders service's database
    type: postgres
    container: postgres
    database: orders
    options: { user: test, password: test }
  orders-events:                # the topics the orders service uses
    type: kafka
    container: kafka
    options: { topics: [orders.placed, payments] }

features:
  paths: [./features]

docs.title: Name resources by whose they are and what they do
docs.text:
A step starts with a resource name, and a reader sees the step long before the config. So the name says whose it is and what role it plays:

Role Name Reads as calls your service orders-client "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" your service's data orders-db, orders-cache "orders-db" table "orders" has "1" rows a broker orders-events (Kafka), orders-queue (RabbitMQ) "orders-events" receives from "orders.placed" stands in for a service you call stripe-stub, catalog-stub "stripe-stub" received "POST" "/v1/charges" object storage invoices-storage "invoices-storage" object "…" should exist

Not api, db, mock or http: those say what kind of thing it is, not whose. Naming resources has the full convention.

docs.title: Features, scenarios and steps
docs.text:
# One feature file per capability of your service
Feature: Placing orders

  # The state every scenario below starts from
  Background:
    Given "orders-db" table "customers" has values:
      | id | email           |
      | 7  | ada@example.com |

  # One behaviour, named as a fact
  Scenario: A placed order is stored and announced
    # When: the one action
    When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
      """
      {"customer_id": 7, "sku": "TMT-01", "qty": 2}
      """
    # Then: what it caused
    Then "orders-client" response status is "201"
    And "orders-db" table "orders" contains:
      | customer_id | sku    | qty | status  |
      | 7           | TMT-01 | 2   | pending |
    And "orders-events" receives from "orders.placed" within "5s"
  • Feature: a file in features/, about one capability of your service.
  • Scenario: one behaviour of that capability, named after the outcome.
  • Background: the starting state every scenario in the file shares. It runs after tomato's reset, before each scenario.
  • Given sets up state, When is the one action, Then checks what it caused.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. One scenario, one behaviour. One When. A scenario that also reads the order back and cancels it fails for three reasons, and tells you none of them.

2. Check the effects, not only the response. A 201 says the service didn't crash. The row in the database, the message on the topic and the file in the bucket are what the rest of your system relies on, so assert them:

Then "orders-client" response status is "201"
And "orders-db" table "orders" has "1" rows
And "orders-events" receives from "orders.placed" within "5s"
# with an s3 resource for the invoices bucket
And "invoices-storage" object "invoices/inv-1.pdf" should exist

3. Split a flow where it crosses a boundary. When the service stores an order, publishes an event, and later consumes another event to mark the order paid, that's two behaviours, so two scenarios: one ends where the service publishes, the next starts where tomato publishes the event the service consumes.

One long scenario A scenario per behaviour orders-clienttomato sends orders APIyour service orders-dbchecks: pending orders-eventsreads · publishes consumeryour service orders-dbchecks: paid tomato drives or checks ityour service one scenario: four reasons to fail, and a wait for the consumer scenario 1: placing an order scenario 2: a payment marks it paid

Tempting: one scenario places the order, waits for the event, publishes the payment and checks the order is paid. It fails for any of four reasons, waits on asynchronous work, and the consumer can't be tested on its own.

Scenario 1 places an order and checks what the service did: the row, and the event on orders.placed. Scenario 2 seeds a pending order, has tomato publish the payment, and checks the service marks it paid. They meet at the topic, and each fails for one reason.

Scenario: Placing an order stores it and announces it
  When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
    """
    {"customer_id": 7, "sku": "TMT-01", "qty": 2}
    """
  Then "orders-client" response status is "201"
  And "orders-db" table "orders" has "1" rows
  And "orders-events" receives from "orders.placed" within "5s"

Scenario: A payment marks the order paid
  Given "orders-db" table "orders" has values:
    | id | customer_id | sku    | qty | status  |
    | 1  | 7           | TMT-01 | 2   | pending |
  When "orders-events" publishes json to "payments":
    """
    {"order_id": 1, "status": "succeeded"}
    """
  Then "orders-db" query "SELECT status FROM orders WHERE id = 1" returns within "10s":
    | status |
    | paid   |

4. Build the state you need. tomato empties every database and topic before every scenario. A scenario that needs an order seeds one in its Given or Background; it never relies on another scenario having run.

5. Variations are more scenarios, not a longer one. The out-of-stock case, the invalid request and the provider being down are behaviours too. Give each its own scenario, or a Scenario Outline when only the values change:

Scenario Outline: An invalid order is refused and nothing is stored
  When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
    """
    <body>
    """
  Then "orders-client" response status is "400"
  And "orders-db" table "orders" is empty

  Examples:
    | body                           |
    | {"sku": "TMT-01", "qty": 2}    |
    | {"customer_id": 7, "qty": 0}   |

Writing a Suite goes deeper into each of these.

docs.title: 5. Check it before you run it
docs.text:
Before running tests, validate your configuration and feature files:

tomato validate

This checks: - Configuration file syntax and structure - Resource type validity - Container references - Feature file parsing - Step definitions availability

Use --plain for CI environments without interactive output:

tomato validate --plain

docs.title: 6. Run it
docs.text:
Run all tests:

tomato run

Run with specific tags:

tomato run --tags "@smoke"

Run with verbose output:

tomato run -v

docs.title: 7. Watch it run
docs.text:
tomato ui opens a local web page that lists the feature files, shows each scenario's steps with the resource every step runs against, and runs scenarios on demand. It watches the feature files and reloads as they change.

tomato ui

It is a development aid, not part of the stable surface: see Stability.

docs.title: Pointing tomato at your application
docs.text:
Tomato can also start your application and connect it to test containers:

# tomato.yml
app:
  command: go run ./cmd/server
  port: 8080
  ready:
    type: http
    path: /health
  wait: 5s
  env:
    DATABASE_URL: "postgres://test:test@{{.postgres.host}}:{{.postgres.port.5432}}/test"
    REDIS_URL: "redis://{{.redis.host}}:{{.redis.port.6379}}"

The {{.container.host}} and {{.container.port.<port>}} templates are replaced with the container's address and its mapped host port. The number is the port inside the container, so {{.postgres.port.5432}} resolves to whichever host port Docker mapped 5432 to. A bare {{.postgres.port}} is left untouched.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Writing a Suite — one behaviour per scenario, and asserting the effects rather than just the response. Read this before you write the second scenario.
  • Configuration Reference — every tomato.yml field
  • Step Reference — every step, grouped by resource
  • Test Coverage — which lines of your service the scenarios ran
  • GitHub Action — running the suite in CI

docs.title: Test coverage
docs.text:
The coverage worth tracking is which lines of your service ran while the scenarios ran. tomato can't see that: it only talks to your service over the network. Your service can. Every mainstream language can measure a running process and write the result when it exits, and tomato starts your service with its environment and stops it cleanly, so turning that on is all it takes.

Language Turn it on Read it Go build with go build -cover, set GOCOVERDIR go tool covdata percent Rust build with RUSTFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage", set LLVM_PROFILE_FILE llvm-profdata, llvm-cov Java, Kotlin, Scala the JaCoCo agent, through JAVA_OPTS or JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS jacococli report Python coverage.py, started by COVERAGE_PROCESS_START coverage combine, coverage report Node.js set NODE_V8_COVERAGE c8 report

Set the variable on the tomato run step, or in your shell: tomato passes its environment to the service, so tomato.yml stays the same with or without coverage.

The one requirement: your service exits cleanly on SIGTERM, within five seconds. That is how tomato stops it, and coverage is written on exit. A service killed instead writes nothing.

Code coverage for black-box tests walks through each language, with the commands, a CI job, and what the number does and doesn't tell you.

docs.title: tomato coverage: a lint for the suite
docs.text:
tomato coverage is something else: it reports which of tomato's steps your feature files use. That says how the suite is worded, not what it tests, so use it as a lint, not a metric:

tomato coverage --format json | jq '.unmatched_steps'
  • unmatched_steps lists steps that match no step definition, usually a typo, before tomato run finds it.
  • A declared resource with no steps used is a resource no scenario checks: a Kafka topic nobody asserts on, say.

Don't gate CI on its percentage. Using ten of the HTTP client's fifty-odd steps can be a complete suite, and the percentage drops whenever tomato adds steps.

Flag Description -c, --config Config file (default tomato.yml) --format text (default), markdown or json --all-types Include every resource type tomato supports, not only those in the config -o, --output Write the report to a file

docs.title: GitHub Action
docs.text: Run Tomato tests in your CI/CD pipeline using the official GitHub Action.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
name: Tests
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Run Tomato Tests
        uses: tomatool/tomato@v2

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Input Description Default version Tomato version (e.g., v1.0.0) Action's tag version config Config file path tomato.yml features Feature files or directories tags Filter by tags (e.g., @smoke and not @slow) scenario Filter by scenario name (regex) verbose Show debug logs false quiet Hide application logs false skip-validate Skip configuration validation before running tests false comment Post/update a test summary comment on the PR true

docs.title: Filter by tags
docs.text:
- uses: tomatool/tomato@v2
  with:
    tags: '@smoke and not @slow'

docs.title: Filter by scenario name
docs.text:
- uses: tomatool/tomato@v2
  with:
    scenario: 'user registration'

docs.title: Run specific features
docs.text:
- uses: tomatool/tomato@v2
  with:
    features: 'features/api features/auth'

docs.title: Verbose output
docs.text:
- uses: tomatool/tomato@v2
  with:
    verbose: 'true'

docs.title: PR comment with test results
docs.text:
- uses: tomatool/tomato@v2
  with:
    comment: 'true'

When enabled on a pull_request workflow, the action posts (or updates) a comment on the PR with a summary of test results — including pass/fail counts and failed scenario details.

Note: The comment feature requires pull-requests: write permission. See the complete workflow example below.

docs.title: Publish a JUnit report
docs.text:
Write a JUnit report from tomato.yml, then upload it or hand it to a test reporter. File outputs are kept when comment is enabled.

# tomato.yml
settings:
  output: "pretty,junit:reports/tomato.xml"

- uses: tomatool/tomato@v2

- name: Upload test report
  if: always()
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: tomato-report
    path: reports/

See Reports for all formats.

docs.title: Pin to specific version
docs.text:
- uses: tomatool/tomato@v2.0.0
  with:
    config: 'tomato.yml'

docs.title: Try an unreleased commit
docs.text:
Used at a commit or a branch instead of a version tag, the action builds tomato from that same commit (with Go, which it sets up), so a change can run in your CI before it is released:

- uses: tomatool/tomato@3f2c1e0d9b8a7f6e5d4c3b2a1f0e9d8c7b6a5f4e
  with:
    config: 'tomato.yml'

Setting version still installs that release instead.

docs.title: Complete workflow example
docs.text:
name: Integration Tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Run Tomato Tests
        uses: tomatool/tomato@v2
        with:
          config: 'tomato.yml'
          verbose: 'true'

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Docker must be available in the runner (default for ubuntu-latest)
  • Repository must contain a valid tomato.yml configuration

docs.title: How to write a tomato suite
docs.text: tomato can run any scenario you write. These are the habits that make the result worth trusting — and the reasoning behind the things tomato refuses to let you do.

docs.title: A scenario covers one behaviour
docs.text:
A scenario earns its place by failing for exactly one reason. When it covers three behaviours, a failure tells you something broke without telling you what, and the second assertion never runs because the first one stopped the scenario.

Not this:

Feature: Orders

  Scenario: Order lifecycle
    When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
      """
      {"sku": "TMT-01", "qty": 2}
      """
    Then "orders-client" response status is "201"
    When "orders-client" sends "GET" to "/orders/1"
    Then "orders-client" response status is "200"
    When "orders-client" sends "DELETE" to "/orders/1"
    Then "orders-client" response status is "204"

This:

Feature: Orders

  Scenario: Placing an order returns it
    When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
      """
      {"sku": "TMT-01", "qty": 2}
      """
    Then "orders-client" response status is "201"

  Scenario: A placed order can be read back
    Given "orders-db" table "orders" has values:
      | id | sku    | qty |
      | 1  | TMT-01 | 2   |
    When "orders-client" sends "GET" to "/orders/1"
    Then "orders-client" response status is "200"

  Scenario: Deleting an order removes it
    Given "orders-db" table "orders" has values:
      | id | sku    | qty |
      | 1  | TMT-01 | 2   |
    When "orders-client" sends "DELETE" to "/orders/1"
    Then "orders-client" response status is "204"
    And "orders-db" table "orders" is empty

The second version is longer and tells you more. Each scenario sets up what it needs, and a failure names the behaviour that broke. They are also independent: the read scenario does not depend on the write scenario having run, so running one of them means something.

If several scenarios need the same starting point, put it in a Background rather than chaining them. tomato runs it after the reset, before each scenario.

docs.title: Assert the effects, not just the response
docs.text:
This is the one that separates a suite that catches regressions from one that does not.

Your application returning 201 says it did not crash. It does not say the order was stored, the event was published, or the receipt was written. Those are the things the rest of your system depends on, and they are exactly what breaks silently.

A response-only scenario:

Feature: Checkout

  Scenario: Placing an order
    When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
      """
      {"sku": "TMT-01", "qty": 2, "email": "ada@example.com"}
      """
    Then "orders-client" response status is "201"

That passes if the handler returns 201 and does nothing else.

The same behaviour, asserted through its effects:

Feature: Checkout

  Scenario: A placed order reaches every dependency
    Given "orders-events" consumes from "order.created"
    When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders" with json:
      """
      {"sku": "TMT-01", "qty": 2, "email": "ada@example.com"}
      """
    Then "orders-client" response status is "201"
    And "orders-db" table "orders" has "1" rows
    And "orders-events" receives from "order.created" within "10s"
    And "receipts-storage" object "receipts/1.pdf" should exist within "10s"

Four assertions, four different systems, one behaviour. If the order lands in the database but the event never publishes, this fails and tells you which.

Two things to note. The consume step comes before the request: a consumer that subscribes afterwards may miss the message. And the effects use within, because an application usually does this work after it has answered — a bare assertion races the write.

docs.title: Every scenario starts from the same state
docs.text:
tomato resets every resource before every scenario. There is no way to turn this off, and that is deliberate: a suite where scenario 7 passes only because scenario 6 ran is a suite that cannot be run in isolation, reordered, or trusted when it goes green.

If a scenario needs a starting state, it declares it:

Feature: Reading an order

  Background:
    Given "orders-db" table "orders" has values:
      | id | sku    | status  |
      | 1  | TMT-01 | shipped |

  Scenario: An existing order is returned
    When "orders-client" sends "GET" to "/orders/1"
    Then "orders-client" response status is "200"
    And "orders-client" response json "status" is "shipped"

A corollary worth knowing: do not assert on generated identifiers you did not set. Sequences, UUIDs and timestamps are not part of the reset contract in every store, and a scenario asserting id is 1 is asserting the order it happens to run in. Seed the id, or assert on something you control.

docs.title: Naming resources
docs.text:
A step is read far more often than the tomato.yml behind it, usually by someone looking at a failure. Its first word is the resource name, so that name has to say what is being talked to without opening the config.

Not this:

Feature: Checkout

  Scenario: A paid order is stored
    Given "mock" stub "POST" "/v1/charges" returns "201"
    When "api" sends "POST" to "/orders"
    Then "db" table "orders" has "1" rows
    And "mock" received "POST" "/v1/charges"

Which API? A mock of what? Whose database? In a suite with two services and three dependencies, every one of those is a guess.

This:

Feature: Checkout

  Scenario: A paid order is stored
    Given "stripe-stub" stub "POST" "/v1/charges" returns "201"
    When "orders-client" sends "POST" to "/orders"
    Then "orders-db" table "orders" has "1" rows
    And "stripe-stub" received "POST" "/v1/charges"

The rule is <name>-<role>, lower-case and hyphenated. <name> is the service, dependency, owner or person; <role> comes from the resource type:

Resource types Role suffix Name is Examples http-client, grpc, websocket-client -client the service it calls, usually the app under test orders-client, catalog-client two clients of one service over different protocols -<protocol>-client orders-http-client, orders-grpc-client http-server, grpc-server, websocket-server -stub the dependency it stands in for stripe-stub, catalog-stub, prices-stub postgres, scylladb -db the owner of the data orders-db redis -cache (-db when it is the primary store) the owner sessions-cache kafka -events the owner or stream orders-events rabbitmq -queue the owner or stream payments-queue s3 -storage the owner invoices-storage browser -browser the person using it alice-browser, shopper-browser shell -cli when it runs one tool, else plain shell the tool todo-cli, shell pdf -pdf the document invoice-pdf aws, lifecycle none: there is one of each aws, lifecycle

A few consequences:

  • Never a bare type or a generic word. Not api, http, client, db, mock, server or grpc: each of them fits every resource of its kind, so it tells the reader nothing.
  • The app under test's client is named after the app: orders-client. Examples with no particular app, like the ones in this documentation's step reference, use app-client.
  • Containers keep naming the software. Entries under containers: — postgres, kafka, minio, chrome — are infrastructure, not roles; only entries under resources: follow this rule.
  • Templates follow the name: {{.stripe-stub.url}}, {{.catalog-stub.address}}. A rename covers tomato.yml, every feature file, and any prose that mentions the resource.

docs.title: A suite is configuration, not code
docs.text:
Everything above is tomato.yml and .feature files. There is no glue code to write, no test harness to maintain, no fixtures library that drifts away from the application.

If you find yourself needing to script around tomato — shelling out to set something up, writing a helper to assert something — that is a gap in tomato, not a gap in your repository. Report it; the fix belongs in tomato as a step, a resource option or a preset, so that everyone gets it.

docs.title: Test it as the thing it is
docs.text:
tomato starts your application the way production does — as a process or a container — and talks to it over the network. It does not import your code, call your functions, or know your framework.

That costs some speed and buys you the thing unit tests cannot give: the scenario exercises your real routing, your real serialisation, your real database driver, against real dependencies in containers. When it passes, the thing that passed is the thing you ship.
